# CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvement for Production Customer-Service Agents

Yanbei Jiang, Chao Lei, Rena Gao, Xiaochen Zhao, Yuchen Ge, Haohang Liu,
Runze Nie, Qitian Chen, Qi An, Haolin Song, Yufei Sun, Yihao Ding, Jey
Han Lau, Krista A. Ehinger, Xingjun Ma, Weijia Chen, Ruiyuan Wu, Zhen
Luo, Ke Xing, Yongjun Yin AI and Data Team, Keeta, Meituan  University
of Melbourne  Fudan University

###### Abstract

Recursive self-improvement (RSI) in production agents involves
transforming accumulated experience into reliable model updates while
adapting to evolving business policies. We present CARE
(Customer-service Agent Retrospective and Evolve), a grounded RSI
framework that operationalizes this process in customer service. Its
goal is to replace a frontier proprietary incumbent with an in-house
mid-sized model that continues learning after deployment. After a
one-time cold start on governed production traces, the current model
serves production traffic alongside the incumbent, and its own failures
drive the next update. A 24/7 inspection process establishes failures
through evidence-blinded, independently reviewed judgments. Attribution
separates model errors from defects in Skills, tools, or the harness,
routing component failures to repair. Model-attributable trajectories
are truncated at the first erroneous decision and paired with verified
repairs. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) then updates the model using
the same model as teacher, with the diagnosis and repair supplied as
privileged information unavailable to the student. To support continued
evolution as business requirements change, training mixes failures from
different Skill/SOP versions, each judged against the policy in force
when it occurred. Candidates run an executable simulation test compiled
from the latest SOP and then frozen, followed by offline inspection of
the resulting traces. Promotion requires a combined
simulation-and-inspection score at least at parity with the deployed
version, confirmation through an online comparison with the incumbent,
and human approval. In a multilingual food-delivery deployment, five RSI
iterations reduce the inspection Bad Case rate of our in-house 31B
model, CARE-31B, from 6.42% after cold start to 1.97%, below the
incumbent GPT-5.4’s 4.60%, raise its simulation accuracy from 93.0% to
94.1%, and bring its online user satisfaction from 4.6 points below the
incumbent to parity (1.7 points above it in the latest period). CARE-31B
also lowers median reply latency by 27.7%, and replacing the incumbent
completely lowers the serving cost per service order by 70.5%.

## 1 Introduction

Large language model (LLM) agents now resolve a substantial share of
customer-service conversations end to end. They interpret user requests,
consult business state through tools, follow a Skill or standard
operating procedure (SOP), and take actions such as refunds,
compensation, or handoff to a human. In many deployments, a frontier
proprietary model powers the agent. This _incumbent_ delivers strong
quality, but serving it at scale is expensive, its inference adds
latency to every turn, and the operator has limited control over its
behavior, update schedule, and data boundaries. These constraints
motivate post-training an _in-house_ mid-sized model that can replace
the incumbent in production.

This replacement requires more than one-time distillation for three
reasons. First, post-training on historical traces leaves a residual
quality gap concentrated in long-tail situations. These failures emerge
only when the model is deployed and encounters the state distribution
induced by its own behavior. Second, the production environment is
non-stationary: Skills and SOPs are revised, tool schemas change, and
prompts are hot-fixed. Behavior that is correct under one configuration
may become incorrect under the next. Third, once the incumbent is
retired its production traces stop, so fresh experience can only come
from the replacement’s own behavior. The replacement must therefore
continue learning from its own experience while adapting to a changing
environment. We frame this requirement as _recursive self-improvement_
(RSI).

The idea of a system that improves the process by which it improves
dates back to [Good \[1\]](#bib.bib25) and was formalized in
self-referential agents such as the Gödel machine \[[2](#bib.bib26)\].
In the LLM era, RSI usually denotes a loop in which a system turns its
own experience and feedback into persistent updates to its components,
including weights, prompts, memory, tools, or harness
code \[[3](#bib.bib14), [4](#bib.bib15), [5](#bib.bib20)\]. Recent
analyses identify the grounding of feedback as a central constraint on
such loops. When the same model generates and evaluates outputs,
correlated errors can reinforce confident mistakes. Recursive training
on self-generated data can also erode the tails of the
distribution \[[6](#bib.bib24)\], and LLM judges can be
gamed \[[7](#bib.bib16), [8](#bib.bib17)\]. Production customer service
compounds these difficulties: there is no verifier that certifies an
entire conversation as correct; a failure may originate in the model, a
Skill, a tool, the harness, the simulator, the judge, or the
infrastructure; and experimentation on real users is constrained.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

$`\pi_{\theta_{0}}`$ from governed production traces of the incumbent

$`\pi_{\theta_{k}}`$ serves part of the production traffic; 24/7 online
inspection turns its own conversations into reviewed failures;
attribution separates model-attributable failures from component
failures, which are repaired outside the model; model-attributable
failures are cut at the first erroneous decision and repaired, and the
model distills from itself on that decision, with the hindsight visible
only to the teacher. The candidate is measured by the evaluation system,
where it runs a simulation test compiled from the latest Skill/SOP and
then frozen, and its simulation traces are inspected offline; it is
promoted only if the combined score of the two is at least at parity
with the deployed version and an online comparison with the incumbent
confirms it. After cold start, training data come from the model’s own
failures and the teacher is the model itself. Stages tagged in red are
driven by an external frontier model rather than by the in-house model.
The operating context is revised independently of the loop: a revision
reaches the deployed model through its input and the evaluation system
through a recompiled test
(Section [3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 What the loop depends on ‣ 3 Problem Formulation ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")).

We present CARE (Customer-service Agent Retrospective and Evolve), a
grounded RSI framework for replacing an incumbent model in production
(Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")).
A one-time cold start (Phase I) builds the initial policy from governed
production traces of the incumbent system, using a data engine that
admits, allocates, and refines conversations.

Thereafter, the improvement loop runs on the in-house model’s own
experience (Phase II). The current model serves part of the production
traffic, and a 24/7 online inspection stage examines its conversations
through evidence-blinded, independently reviewed judgments. For each
confirmed failure, an attribution stage determines whether
responsibility lies with the model or a non-model component. Component
failures are repaired outside the model. For each model-attributable
failure, the trajectory is truncated at the first erroneous decision and
a verified repair is constructed. The model then evolves through
on-policy self-distillation (OPSD): the student samples its own decision
at that point, while the same model serves as the teacher with access to
the diagnosis and verified repair as privileged information.

A separate evaluation system determines whether the candidate is ready
to replace the deployed version. The candidate runs an executable
simulation test compiled from the latest Skill/SOP and then frozen;
offline inspection evaluates the resulting simulation traces. Its
combined score must be at least at parity with the deployed version
before an online comparison with the incumbent. Failures used for
learning and cases used for evaluation come from separate sources and
are never mixed. After cold start, the model’s own failures supply the
training data, and the model itself supplies the teacher.

The loop is not free of external intervention. An external frontier
model, not the in-house model, drives online inspection, attribution,
and repair construction; component owners repair non-model failures; and
a person approves each release. The external model’s output reaches
training only as privileged information for the teacher, so CARE is
self-improving in the source of its experience and of its teacher, not
in the sense of running without outside help. The operating context also
changes independently of the loop: Skills and SOPs can be revised at any
time, including while a version is serving. Until the next update the
deployed model has to follow a revision from its input alone, which is
why training mixes several policy versions, and each simulation test is
compiled from the current version.
Section [3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 What the loop depends on ‣ 3 Problem Formulation ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")
sets out both points.

In Phase II, the reliance on self-generated training data and teacher
supervision introduces a risk of error amplification, when
model-generated outputs are evaluated without independent verification.
Three checks outside the model therefore govern the loop. Reviewed
evidence, rather than a single judge score, establishes whether a
production conversation contains a failure. Attribution determines
whether that failure warrants a model update or a component repair. In
simulation, executed business state establishes whether an action such
as a refund or cancellation actually occurred, independently of the
model’s description of that action. Attribution also supplies privileged
information for self-distillation: the teacher’s information advantage
comes from being told what went wrong, not from critiquing its own
output.

Our contributions are as follows.

1.  1.  Problem formulation. We formalize production model replacement as
        grounded RSI, with an explicit replacement criterion and an
        iteration in which the model supplies both its experience and its
        teacher
        (Section [3](#S3 "3 Problem Formulation ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")).
2.  2.  Grounded retrospection and evaluation. A 24/7, layered,
        evidence-blinded online inspection process and a failure-attribution
        stage separate model errors from component errors before learning
        (Section [5](#S5 "5 Retrospection: Online Inspection and Attribution ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")).
        A separate evaluation system assesses every candidate through an
        executable, partially observable simulation test and offline
        inspection of the resulting traces
        (Section [7](#S7 "7 Evaluation System and Promotion ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")).
3.  3.  Attribution-guided on-policy self-distillation. We truncate each
        attributed failure trajectory at its first erroneous decision,
        construct a verified minimal repair using hindsight information, and
        train the model on its own outputs at the identified erroneous
        decision under the supervision of a hindsight-informed self-teacher.
        Hindsight information is excluded from the student’s input. Training
        incorporates failures from different Skill/SOP versions, each
        evaluated against its corresponding SOP, to improve the model’s
        ability to make decisions consistent with the provided policy
        (Section [6](#S6 "6 Phase II: Evolve by Attribution-Guided On-Policy Self-Distillation ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")).
4.  4.  Production study. We report results from a multilingual
        food-delivery customer-service deployment covering seven regions,
        including comparisons with frontier models, online A/B comparisons,
        five RSI iterations that produce six model versions, and ablations
        of the learning signal and of the OPSD loss
        (Section [8](#S8 "8 Experiments ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")).

Over five iterations, the inspection Bad Case rate of our in-house 31B
model, CARE-31B, decreases from 6.42% after cold start to 1.97%, less
than half of the incumbent’s 4.60% and the lowest rate among all
evaluated models. Simulation accuracy improves from 93.0% to 94.1%,
behind the incumbent and Gemini-3.5-Flash, and the combined evaluation
score reaches 96.07 against the incumbent’s 96.10. In the online
deployment across all seven regions, user satisfaction improves from 4.6
percentage points below the incumbent at cold start to comparable
performance in the final two versions (+0.3 and +1.7 points).

These results highlight the limitations of cold start alone. Although
the cold-start model completes substantially more simulated cases than
the untuned base model, it produces more confirmed failures than both
the base model and the incumbent. Recursive self-improvement addresses
this gap through iterative refinement.

The ablations show why the learning signal matters at this data scale.
On a small increment of repairs, supervised fine-tuning collapses during
training, and preference optimization collapses into immediate handoff,
passing 15.1% of simulated cases. OPSD keeps a simulation accuracy of
94.1%. Among its loss configurations, a forward KL divergence truncated
to the teacher’s top 32 tokens performs best overall and is the one
deployed.

Section [2](#S2 "2 Background and Related Work ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")
positions CARE within the RSI literature.
Section [3](#S3 "3 Problem Formulation ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")
formalizes the setting.
Sections [4](#S4 "4 Phase I: Cold Start from Production Traces ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")–[7](#S7 "7 Evaluation System and Promotion ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")

## 2 Background and Related Work

### 2.1 Recursive Self-Improvement

[Good \[1\]](#bib.bib25) introduced the concept of an “intelligence
explosion,” in which a machine improves the design of its successors.
The Gödel machine \[[2](#bib.bib26)\] formalized a self-referential
agent capable of modifying its own code upon proving the benefits of
such modifications. Contemporary recursive self-improvement (RSI)
extends these ideas to systems that iteratively update their components
through accumulated experience and feedback \[[3](#bib.bib14),
[4](#bib.bib15), [5](#bib.bib20), [9](#bib.bib21)\]. Existing approaches
differ in their update mechanisms and supervision signals. STaR improves
reasoning through self-generated rationales leading to correct
answers \[[10](#bib.bib23)\], SPIN learns from comparisons between
model-generated responses and human demonstrations \[[11](#bib.bib13)\],
and Self-Rewarding Language Models use model-generated judgments to
improve both the policy and its reward model \[[12](#bib.bib12)\].
Beyond model parameters, Reflexion incorporates verbal feedback into
subsequent attempts \[[13](#bib.bib8)\], Voyager accumulates executable
skills through environment interaction \[[14](#bib.bib11)\], and the
Darwin Gödel Machine evolves agent code through empirical
evaluation \[[15](#bib.bib9)\].

The reliability of self-generated feedback remains a central challenge
in RSI. Shared biases between generators and evaluators can reinforce
existing errors, while recursive training on generated data may lead to
model collapse \[[6](#bib.bib24)\]. Previous studies also report high
variance, task-order sensitivity, and vulnerabilities in LLM-based
evaluation \[[8](#bib.bib17), [7](#bib.bib16)\]. Formal verification and
execution feedback provide more direct evidence of correctness than
model-generated judgments alone \[[5](#bib.bib20)\]. A recent
taxonomy \[[5](#bib.bib20)\] distinguishes _bounded_ self-improvement,
where updates are evaluated against fixed external criteria, from
_open-ended_ RSI, which can also modify the mechanisms governing
improvement. It further categorizes improvement loops according to human
involvement: _human-in-the-loop_ systems require human review of
individual updates, _human-on-the-loop_ systems automate improvement
while retaining human oversight and deployment control, and
_closed-loop_ systems operate without human intervention. Within this
taxonomy, CARE adopts a bounded, human-on-the-loop approach in which
retrospection, error attribution, and model training operate
automatically, while promotion to production remains subject to
evaluation and deployment gates. Learning signals are grounded in
simulated business-state transitions, reviewed inspections, and verified
repairs, while failures attributed to non-model components are directed
to component repair.

### 2.2 On-Policy and Privileged-Information Distillation

On-policy learning addresses compounding errors arising from the
mismatch between training distributions and states encountered during
execution \[[16](#bib.bib28)\]. Generalized Knowledge Distillation (GKD)
extends this principle to language models by sampling sequences from the
student and minimizing divergence from teacher
predictions \[[17](#bib.bib22)\]. Recent research further examines the
training dynamics and practical considerations of on-policy distillation
for LLMs \[[18](#bib.bib6)\]. Learning Using Privileged Information
(LUPI) introduces supervision from information available during training
but inaccessible during inference \[[19](#bib.bib27)\]. Privileged
Information Distillation extends this principle to multi-turn agents,
where a teacher conditioned on privileged actions guides a student
without access to those actions \[[20](#bib.bib7)\]. On-Policy
Self-Distillation (OPSD) enables a single model to serve as both teacher
and student, using verified reasoning traces in the teacher context to
minimize token-level divergence on student-generated
trajectories \[[21](#bib.bib19)\].

CARE adopts the self-distillation framework of OPSD while introducing
failure-specific hindsight as privileged information. Unlike approaches
using reference solutions or privileged actions, the self-teacher
receives a reviewed, causally attributed diagnosis and a verified
minimal repair at the first erroneous decision. The student learns from
its own decision outputs under hindsight-informed supervision without
access to hindsight in its input. This enables recursive model
improvement through verified supervision derived from the model’s own
production failures.

### 2.3 Interactive Evaluation and Continual Adaptation

Interactive agent evaluation examines decision-making through multi-turn
interactions, tool execution, and environment-state transitions.
$`\tau`$-bench evaluates tool–agent–user interactions under
domain-specific policies \[[22](#bib.bib1)\], while $`\tau^{2}`$-bench
extends this setting to environments where both users and agents can
modify shared state \[[23](#bib.bib2)\]. These benchmarks motivate the
explicit state transitions and outcome verification adopted by the CARE
simulator. Agent Lightning and DataEnvGym further investigate the
separation of agent execution from training and data-generation
infrastructure \[[24](#bib.bib3), [25](#bib.bib4)\].

Continual learning introduces challenges including catastrophic
forgetting, distribution shift, and evaluation leakage during successive
model updates \[[26](#bib.bib10)\]. Production agents face an additional
challenge as business policies evolve independently of model updates.
CARE addresses this setting by incorporating failure trajectories from
different Skill/SOP versions, with each trajectory evaluated against the
SOP applicable during its execution. This enables the model to learn
decisions consistent with the provided policy rather than relying on
fixed policy-specific behaviors.

Table [1](#S2.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 2.3 Interactive Evaluation and Continual Adaptation ‣ 2 Background and Related Work ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")
