## 3 Problem Formulation

### 3.1 Agents, policies in context, and the incumbent

A customer-service agent operates under business rules specified through
its input rather than fixed within the model parameters. We define the
_operating context_ as

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       c=(s,\,w,\,p),
       ```             |     | (1) |

where $`s`$ denotes the Skill/SOP governing agent behavior, $`w`$ the
available tools and their schemas, and $`p`$ the prompting instructions.
The correct action for a given request depends on the operating context,
as different Skills/SOPs and tool configurations may impose different
requirements and constraints. As Skills and SOPs evolve during
operation, the operating context changes accordingly.

An interaction under operating context $`c`$ generates a trajectory

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       \tau=(x_{0},o_{1},a_{1},y_{1},\ldots,o_{T},a_{T},y_{T},z),
       ```                                                         |     | (2) |

where $`x_{0}`$ denotes the initial business state (e.g., order,
delivery, or after-sales status), $`o_{t}`$ the agent-visible
observation, $`a_{t}`$ the agent’s action (e.g., a response, tool query,
or business operation), $`y_{t}`$ the corresponding tool or environment
result, and $`z`$ the terminal business outcome. The agent follows a
policy $`\pi(a_{t}\mid h_{t},c)`$, which determines the next action
given the agent-visible interaction history $`h_{t}`$ and operating
context $`c`$. We denote the incumbent model serving production by
$`\pi^{\star}`$ and the in-house model by $`\pi_{\theta}`$, initialized
from an open-weight base model with parameters
$`\theta_{\mathrm{base}}`$.

The incumbent serves three roles: its production trajectories provide
the initial training data for cold start, its measured performance
establishes the replacement benchmark, and it remains available as a
fallback during model promotion. Beyond these roles, the incumbent is
not used to generate training labels during recursive self-improvement.

### 3.2 Replacement and improvement criteria

Let $`Q(\pi,c)`$ denote the expected business and service quality under
operating context $`c`$, $`H(\pi,c)`$ the rate of hard violations (e.g.,
prohibited actions or invalid state transitions), and $`K(\pi)`$ the
average serving cost per interaction. We define the replacement criteria
separately for each operating context rather than aggregating
performance across contexts.

###### Definition 1 (Replacement).

An in-house policy $`\pi_{\theta}`$ satisfies the replacement criteria
relative to the incumbent $`\pi^{\star}`$ over a context set
$`\mathcal{C}`$, with quality tolerance $`\delta\geq 0`$, if, for every
$`c\in\mathcal{C}`$,

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
Q(\pi_{\theta},c)\geq Q(\pi^{\star},c)-\delta,\qquad H(\pi_{\theta},c)\leq H(\pi^{\star},c),\qquad K(\pi_{\theta})<K(\pi^{\star}).
``` |  | (3) |

These criteria define the model replacement objective rather than the
evaluation procedure for individual updates. Continued improvement
remains necessary as new failures emerge and business policies evolve
during deployment.

###### Definition 2 (Grounded RSI iteration).

Given the current model parameters $`\theta_{k}`$, an iteration of CARE
generates experience $`\mathcal{T}_{k}\sim\pi_{\theta_{k}}`$ and
produces a candidate model through

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{k}`$ | $`\displaystyle=(\mathrm{Construct}\circ\mathrm{Attribute}\circ\mathrm{Retrospect})(\mathcal{T}_{k}),`$ |  | (4) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\theta^{\prime}_{k}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\mathrm{Evolve}(\theta_{k};\mathcal{D}_{k}),`$ |  |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle\theta_{k+1}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\theta^{\prime}_{k},&\text{if }\mathrm{Gate}(\theta^{\prime}_{k},\theta_{k})=1,\\
\theta_{k},&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}`$ |  |  |

The current model generates the training experience and serves as the
self-teacher during evolution. External information provides grounding
through executed business states, reviewed evidence, and verified
repairs, with hindsight available only to the teacher. The binary
promotion gate accepts a candidate if its combined offline score meets
or exceeds that of the deployed model, an online comparison with the
incumbent confirms its suitability, and human approval is obtained. The
combined score incorporates simulation accuracy on a test set compiled
from the latest Skill/SOP and frozen for candidate evaluation, together
with offline inspection of the resulting simulation trajectories
(Section [7](#S7 "7 Evaluation System and Promotion ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents"),
Eq. ([46](#S7.E46 "In 7.4 Promotion ‣ 7 Evaluation System and Promotion ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents"))).

Definition [2](#Thmdefinition2 "Definition 2 (Grounded RSI iteration). ‣ 3.2 Replacement and improvement criteria ‣ 3 Problem Formulation ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")
specifies what “self” means in CARE: the model supplies both the
training experience and the self-teacher, while external evidence and
verification establish the correctness of the learning signals. Each
promoted iteration is subject to independent evaluation and controlled
deployment.

### 3.3 What the loop depends on

#### External intervention.

Definition [2](#Thmdefinition2 "Definition 2 (Grounded RSI iteration). ‣ 3.2 Replacement and improvement criteria ‣ 3 Problem Formulation ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")
is narrower than a loop that improves without external intervention. The
in-house model supplies the experience and the teacher, but
$`\mathrm{Retrospect}`$, $`\mathrm{Attribute}`$, and
$`\mathrm{Construct}`$ in
Eq. ([4](#S3.E4 "In Definition 2 (Grounded RSI iteration). ‣ 3.2 Replacement and improvement criteria ‣ 3 Problem Formulation ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents"))
are driven by an external frontier model, such as GPT, rather than by
$`\pi_{\theta}`$. People also take part: component owners and engineers
repair non-model failures, cases that cannot be confirmed may go to
manual review, and a person approves each promotion. The external
model’s output reaches training only as privileged information for the
self-teacher, and the student never sees it
(Section [6.2](#S6.SS2 "6.2 Hindsight as privileged information ‣ 6 Phase II: Evolve by Attribution-Guided On-Policy Self-Distillation ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")).
We keep these stages outside the in-house model because a model that
identifies and diagnoses its own failures would reinforce its own
errors; independent judgment is what grounds the loop. CARE is therefore
self-improving in its weights and training experience, not autonomous.

#### Changes to the operating context.

A change of $`c`$ is not a step of the loop. Business owners revise
Skills, SOPs, tools, and prompts on their own schedule, and the
component repairs that attribution triggers change them too, so a
revision can land at any stage of an iteration. It reaches the loop in
three places. While a version is serving, a revision reaches the model
through its input and the weights stay the same, so until the next
iteration the deployed model has to adapt by following the policy it is
given. If it fails, online inspection picks the failure up and judges it
against the revised policy, so the next iteration learns from it. During
construction and training, each failure keeps the context in which it
occurred, and a training set mixes several policy versions so that the
model learns to follow the policy it is given and to generalize across
revisions
(Section [6.3](#S6.SS3 "6.3 Data selection and mixing across policy versions ‣ 6 Phase II: Evolve by Attribution-Guided On-Policy Self-Distillation ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")).
During evaluation, the simulation test is compiled automatically from
the current Skill/SOP and then frozen, so a candidate is measured
against the policy in force
(Section [7](#S7 "7 Evaluation System and Promotion ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")).

### 3.4 Requirements of grounded RSI in production

Reliable improvement under
Eq. ([4](#S3.E4 "In Definition 2 (Grounded RSI iteration). ‣ 3.2 Replacement and improvement criteria ‣ 3 Problem Formulation ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents"))
depends on the validity of the feedback, attribution, learning, and
evaluation processes. We identify four requirements for grounded RSI in
production, each addressed by a component of CARE.

#### R1: Grounded failure identification.

Customer-service interactions lack a universal correctness verifier,
making failure identification dependent on executed business states and
independently reviewed evidence. Reliable retrospection requires
distinguishing confirmed failures from inconclusive judgments while
preventing evaluation shortcuts arising from model identities, prior
quality labels, or other source metadata. Independence between training
failures and evaluation cases is further required to avoid evaluation
leakage
(Sections [5](#S5 "5 Retrospection: Online Inspection and Attribution ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")
and [7](#S7 "7 Evaluation System and Promotion ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")).

#### R2: Causal attribution before learning.

A failed interaction may originate from model behavior, defective Skills
or prompts, tool or routing errors, simulator artifacts, judge errors,
or infrastructure failures. These causes require different corrective
interventions, and treating them uniformly as model errors can encourage
the model to compensate for defective components. Reliable learning
therefore depends on attributing failures to their underlying causes and
restricting model updates to failures attributable to model behavior
(Section [5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2 Failure attribution ‣ 5 Retrospection: Online Inspection and Attribution ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")).

#### R3: Learning from self-generated failures without reinforcing errors.

Confirmed failures provide evidence of incorrect execution, whereas
effective model improvement depends on identifying the first erroneous
decision and constructing a verified repair. Directly incorporating
failed trajectories into training risks propagating the errors embedded
in those trajectories. Reliable on-policy learning therefore requires
supervision grounded in verified repairs, applied to the model’s own
generated decisions, with privileged hindsight accessible exclusively to
the self-teacher
(Section [6.2](#S6.SS2 "6.2 Hindsight as privileged information ‣ 6 Phase II: Evolve by Attribution-Guided On-Policy Self-Distillation ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")).

#### R4: Policy-conditioned learning and safe promotion.

Evolving Skills and SOPs introduce policy variations across trajectories
collected during successive iterations, such that similar interactions
may require different actions under different policy versions. Learning
without accounting for these variations risks reinforcing decisions that
are inconsistent with the operating context. Policy-conditioned learning
therefore preserves the Skill/SOP associated with each failure and
verifies its corresponding repair against the policy in force at the
time, enabling training across multiple policy versions
(Section [6.3](#S6.SS3 "6.3 Data selection and mixing across policy versions ‣ 6 Phase II: Evolve by Attribution-Guided On-Policy Self-Distillation ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")).
Reliable promotion further requires evaluating candidate models on a
simulation test compiled from the latest Skill/SOP and frozen for
candidate evaluation, followed by offline inspection of the resulting
trajectories, online comparison with the incumbent, and human approval
(Section [7](#S7 "7 Evaluation System and Promotion ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")).

## 4 Phase I: Cold Start from Production Traces

Cold start produces the initial policy $`\pi_{\theta_{0}}`$ that enters
the recursive loop. Its raw material is the logged production behavior
of the incumbent system: complete agent conversations with tool
definitions, calls, results, and Skill content, together with
conversations handled by human support staff. These logs are abundant
but uneven. They contain execution defects, language errors, and
scenario imbalance, and an incumbent trace that *looks* fluent may still
take an action that contradicts the business state. We therefore treat
cold start as a data-governance problem with three separate decisions
(Figure [2](#S4.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 4 Phase I: Cold Start from Production Traces ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")):
which conversations are admissible as positive demonstrations, how a
fixed training budget is allocated among them, and whether their wording
can be improved without changing their behavior. For raw candidates
$`D`$, admitted candidates $`D_{s}`$, selected members $`S`$, and
retained output $`F`$, the engine enforces

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\operatorname{IDs}(F)\subseteq\operatorname{IDs}(S)\subseteq\operatorname{IDs}(D_{s})\subseteq\operatorname{IDs}(D),
``` |  | (5) |

so later stages can only remove members, never introduce new ones.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 2: The cold-start data engine. (a) Admission keeps complete,
context-keyed conversations that pass language, structural, and
evidence-anchored semantic checks; only no_problem conversations enter
$`D_{s}`$, and rejected or unresolved records are never backfilled. (b)
Allocation splits a fixed budget $`N`$ over region groups, the scenarios
of each group, and the regions of GCC4, applying the
capacity-constrained equal split of
Eq. [8](#S4.E8 "In Capacity-constrained equal split. ‣ 4.2 Hierarchical, capacity-constrained allocation ‣ 4 Phase I: Cold Start from Production Traces ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")
at every level, and then freezes the selected members $`S`$. (c)
Refinement borrows tone from linked human conversations for eligible
turns while preserving every protected field; a rejected rewrite keeps
the original conversation, and only a failed final check removes it.

### 4.1 Admission

The learning unit is a complete conversation rather than an isolated
reply, because a reply that is appropriate in one business state can be
wrong in another. Exports may contain several cumulative snapshots of
one conversation; the engine keeps the most complete snapshot,
deduplicates by conversation identity, normalizes region, scenario, and
provenance, and attaches the context key $`c`$ of
Eq. ([1](#S3.E1 "In 3.1 Agents, policies in context, and the incumbent ‣ 3 Problem Formulation ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")).

#### Language consistency.

Multilingual customer service introduces language-related defects,
including unintended script mixing, word-internal concatenation, and
intrusion of unrelated languages. A rule-based detector identifies
potentially anomalous spans in assistant messages, which are
subsequently evaluated by a model using the surrounding conversational
context. Protocol fields, URLs, placeholders, brand names, and
user-initiated code-switching are excluded from defect classification.
Conversations with confirmed or unresolved language issues are excluded
from the admitted pool.

#### Structural quality.

Deterministic checks then filter scenario scope, validate action chains,
and compute context length with the target tokenizer and chat template,
including tool definitions. Over-length conversations are excluded
rather than truncated, since truncation silently changes the decision
problem. Known risk patterns, such as inappropriate handoff placement,
formulaic online-presence confirmations, claims of real-time processing,
and placeholder images, are removed at this stage.

#### Evidence-anchored semantic screening.

Structural validity alone provides insufficient evidence of behavioral
correctness. A screening model examines every structurally qualified
conversation, including tool execution results and structured business
facts, to identify execution defects supported by identifiable evidence.
Representative cases include applying a missing-item procedure to a
whole-order non-receipt request and claiming courier contact without a
corresponding executed action. Weak indicators, including low customer
satisfaction, prolonged interactions, and requests for human assistance,
provide insufficient grounds for confirming a defect. Each conversation
$`x`$ receives a verdict
$`V(x)\in\{\texttt{no\_problem},\texttt{problem},\texttt{inconclusive}\}`$,
where inconclusive denotes cases whose classification depends on
unavailable runtime evidence. Admission is restricted to conversations
classified as no_problem:

|     |                                                 |     |     |
|-----|-------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       D_{s}=\{x\in D_{q}:V(x)=\texttt{no\_problem}\},
       ```                                              |     | (6) |

where $`D_{q}`$ denotes the structurally qualified candidate pool.
Semantic screening is applied to the complete candidate pool before
allocation, ensuring that training quotas are determined from admitted
conversations. The screening procedure prioritizes precision in
identifying problem cases, treating the configured problem-rate limit as
a ceiling rather than a target.

### 4.2 Hierarchical, capacity-constrained allocation

Production traffic is dominated by a few regions and scenarios; in an
early snapshot, one scenario alone accounted for 37.8% of the
conversations. Sampling according to the empirical traffic distribution
would therefore underrepresent low-frequency regions and scenarios.
Allocation assigns a fixed budget $`N`$ hierarchically: first across
four region groups (Saudi Arabia, Brazil, Hong Kong, and a GCC4 group of
the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Kuwait, and Qatar), then across the
scenarios present in each group, and finally across the individual
regions within each group–scenario cell, limiting the dominance of
high-volume categories.

#### Cells and capacities.

Every admitted conversation $`x\in D_{s}`$ carries a cell key
$`\kappa(x)=(g,\sigma,r)`$: its region group
$`g\in\mathcal{G}=\{\mathrm{SA},\mathrm{BR},\mathrm{HK},\mathrm{GCC4}\}`$,
its scenario $`\sigma`$, and its region $`r\in\mathcal{R}_{g}`$, where
$`\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{GCC4}}=\{\mathrm{AE},\mathrm{BH},\mathrm{KW},\mathrm{QA}\}`$
and every other group contains a single region. The admitted capacity of
each cell and its marginals are

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
c_{g\sigma r}=\bigl|\{x\in D_{s}:\kappa(x)=(g,\sigma,r)\}\bigr|,\qquad c_{g\sigma}=\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}_{g}}c_{g\sigma r},\qquad c_{g}=\sum_{\sigma}c_{g\sigma}.
``` |  | (7) |

#### Capacity-constrained equal split.

The same capacity-constrained allocation principle is applied at each
hierarchical level. For a budget $`M`$ and capacities
$`\mathbf{c}=(c_{1},\dots,c_{K})`$, the continuous water-filling
solution $`\mathbf{n}^{*}=(n_{1}^{*},\dots,n_{K}^{*})`$ satisfies

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
n_{j}^{*}=\min(c_{j},\lambda),\qquad 0\leq n_{j}^{*}\leq c_{j},\qquad\sum_{j=1}^{K}n_{j}^{*}=M,
``` |  | (8) |

where the water level $`\lambda`$ solves
$`\sum_{j}\min(c_{j},\lambda)=M`$. A scarce category contributes its
entire available capacity, and the remaining budget is distributed
equally among categories with residual capacity. The corresponding
integer allocation operator $`\mathrm{WF}(M;\mathbf{c})`$ implements
this principle through the sequential assignment procedure described
below. The operator is applied hierarchically as follows:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
(n_{g})_{g}=\mathrm{WF}\bigl(N;(c_{g})_{g}\bigr),\qquad(n_{g\sigma})_{\sigma}=\mathrm{WF}\bigl(n_{g};(c_{g\sigma})_{\sigma}\bigr),\qquad(n_{g\sigma r})_{r}=\mathrm{WF}\bigl(n_{g\sigma};(c_{g\sigma r})_{r}\bigr).
``` |  | (9) |

$`\mathrm{WF}(M;\mathbf{c})`$ is feasible if and only if
$`M\leq\sum_{j}c_{j}`$. Each parent capacity is the sum of its
children’s capacities
(Eq. ([7](#S4.E7 "In Cells and capacities. ‣ 4.2 Hierarchical, capacity-constrained allocation ‣ 4 Phase I: Cold Start from Production Traces ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents"))),
and the constraints $`n_{g}\leq c_{g}`$ and
$`n_{g\sigma}\leq c_{g\sigma}`$ ensure the feasibility of every
subsequent allocation. Consequently, the overall selection is feasible
if and only if $`|D_{s}|\geq N`$. If $`|D_{s}|<N`$, selection fails
rather than reducing the specified training budget. A category with
$`c_{j}=0`$ receives zero allocation, reflecting the coverage
limitations of the admitted pool.

#### Integer assignment.

The implementation assigns slots sequentially, prioritizing categories
with remaining capacity and the smallest current allocation. The
resulting integer quotas satisfy

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
n_{k}-n_{j}\geq 2\;\Longrightarrow\;n_{j}=c_{j},\qquad\forall j,k.
``` |  | (10) |

A category can therefore trail another by two or more slots only after
exhausting its available capacity, while categories with remaining
capacity differ by at most one slot. When category $`k`$ received its
last slot, any category $`j`$ with fewer assigned slots and unused
capacity would have been selected first. This establishes max–min
fairness under capacity constraints. Proportional sampling,
$`n_{j}=Mc_{j}/\sum_{k}c_{k}`$, would instead reproduce the traffic
skew, assigning a scenario that accounts for 37.8% of conversations the
same proportion of the training budget.

#### Member selection.

The allocation determines the number of conversations contributed by
each cell, while secondary criteria determine the selected members:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
S=\bigcup_{g,\sigma,r}S_{g\sigma r},\qquad S_{g\sigma r}\subseteq\{x\in D_{s}:\kappa(x)=(g,\sigma,r)\},\qquad|S_{g\sigma r}|=n_{g\sigma r},
``` |  | (11) |

so $`|S|=N`$. Records are selected without duplication
($`n_{g\sigma r}\leq c_{g\sigma r}`$), and quarantined records are
excluded from backfilling ($`S\subseteq D_{s}`$). Secondary criteria,
including handoff stage, data source, and multimodal content, determine
membership within each cell while preserving the allocated quotas. The
availability of linked human references and eligibility for subsequent
expression refinement are excluded from selection criteria to prevent
refinement opportunities from influencing training exposure. The
selected set $`S`$ is then frozen as the training membership.

### 4.3 State-aligned expression refinement

Incumbent responses generally follow the intended business procedures,
although their linguistic expression can be formulaic, particularly when
addressing customer frustration. Human support conversations provide
more natural expressions of empathy and reassurance, while differing in
operational permissions and workflow states. We therefore use human
conversations exclusively as references for linguistic expression,
preserving the business facts and actions of the original agent
trajectories. Refinement operates on the frozen selected set $`S`$.

#### Representation.

We represent a selected conversation as
$`\tau=\bigl((z_{1},u_{1}),\dots,(z_{L},u_{L})\bigr)`$, where $`z_{i}`$
contains the protected fields of message $`i`$, including roles,
actions, FAQ codes, responsibility assignments, action extensions, and
tool calls and results, while $`u_{i}`$ denotes its natural-language
content. The projection onto protected fields,
$`P(\tau)=(z_{1},\dots,z_{L})`$, additionally preserves the number and
order of messages.

#### Reference labeling.

Let $`\tau^{\mathrm{h}}`$ denote a human support conversation linked to
$`\tau`$ through an explicit conversation key. Ambiguous links are
excluded from reference matching, while conversations without valid
references retain their original expressions. For an assistant message
$`i`$ in $`\tau`$ and a human response $`v\in\tau^{\mathrm{h}}`$, a
labeling model determines their alignment in business state and action,
$`\alpha(v,i;\tau)\in\{0,1\}`$. The eligible references are

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
R_{i}(\tau)=\bigl\{v\in\tau^{\mathrm{h}}\setminus\mathcal{X}:\;\alpha(v,i;\tau)=1\bigr\},
``` |  | (12) |

where $`\mathcal{X}`$ comprises rating solicitations, closing and
repetitive templates, empty apologies, self-introductions, and private
content. An alignment label $`\alpha=1`$ indicates eligibility as a
linguistic style reference, with business facts retained exclusively
from the original agent trajectory.

#### Eligible targets.

Refinement is restricted to existing assistant messages with at least
one eligible reference:

|     |                                                       |     |      |
|-----|-------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       T(\tau)=\bigl\{i:\;R_{i}(\tau)\neq\varnothing\bigr\}.
       ```                                                    |     | (13) |

#### Constrained rewrite.

For $`T(\tau)\neq\varnothing`$, the rewriting model proposes
$`\tau^{\prime}`$ through local modifications to eligible message text,
$`u^{\prime}_{i}=f\bigl(u_{i};\tau,R_{i}(\tau)\bigr)`$ for
$`i\in T(\tau)`$. The rewriting process preserves the original message
structure, actions, and tool interactions by enforcing

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
P(\tau^{\prime})=P(\tau),\qquad\{i:u^{\prime}_{i}\neq u_{i}\}\subseteq T(\tau).
``` |  | (14) |

A validation gate $`\gamma(\tau,\tau^{\prime})\in\{0,1\}`$ assesses
reference reliability, expected linguistic improvement, and potential
risks introduced by the rewrite. Rejected proposals revert to the
original conversation:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\tilde{\tau}=\begin{cases}\tau^{\prime}&\text{if }T(\tau)\neq\varnothing\text{ and }\gamma(\tau,\tau^{\prime})=1,\\
\tau&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}
``` |  | (15) |

#### Final check.

Preservation of structural fields alone is insufficient to establish
semantic equivalence. The refinement process therefore recomputes
context length and derived attributes and repeats the language and
structural checks of
Section [4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Admission ‣ 4 Phase I: Cold Start from Production Traces ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents"),
including model-based language adjudication where applicable. Let
$`q(\tilde{\tau})\in\{0,1\}`$ denote the final quality check. The
retained corpus is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
F=\bigl\{\tilde{\tau}:\;\tau\in S,\;q(\tilde{\tau})=1\bigr\},\qquad n^{F}_{g\sigma r}=\bigl|\{\tilde{\tau}\in F:\kappa(\tilde{\tau})=(g,\sigma,r)\}\bigr|\leq n_{g\sigma r}.
``` |  | (16) |

Rejected rewrites retain their original conversations
(Eq. ([15](#S4.E15 "In Constrained rewrite. ‣ 4.3 State-aligned expression refinement ‣ 4 Phase I: Cold Start from Production Traces ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents"))),
whereas failures in the final quality check result in exclusion.
Consequently, $`F`$ satisfies the membership constraint of
Eq. ([5](#S4.E5 "In 4 Phase I: Cold Start from Production Traces ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")).
The absence of resampling allows the retained cell distribution
$`n^{F}`$ to deviate from the original allocation quotas, which are
reported separately.

### 4.4 Cold-start objective

The retained set $`F`$ forms the cold-start corpus $`D_{0}`$. Starting
from $`\theta_{\mathrm{base}}`$, the instruction-tuned Gemma-4-31B-IT
checkpoint, we minimize the masked negative log-likelihood

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cold}}(\theta)=-\frac{1}{Z}\sum_{i\in D_{0}}\sum_{j}m_{ij}\,\log\pi_{\theta}\bigl(y_{ij}\mid y_{i,<j},c_{i}\bigr),\qquad Z=\sum_{i,j}m_{ij},
``` |  | (17) |

where $`m_{ij}`$ selects assistant tokens. System-injected context
cards, tool results, and business state serve as conditioning inputs;
supervision begins with the first assistant response or tool call
following the first user message. This objective trains the model to
generate actions and responses conditioned on the supplied Skills, tool
contracts, and business context, providing a context-dependent
initialization for subsequent recursive improvement.

The training configuration of this stage is provided in
Appendix [A.3](#A1.SS3 "A.3 Training configuration ‣ Appendix A Cold-Start Details ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents"),
while historical revisions of the data preparation process, including
earlier approaches that concatenated or inserted human turns, are
documented in
Appendix [A.1](#A1.SS1 "A.1 Evolution of the data recipe ‣ Appendix A Cold-Start Details ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents").

## 5 Retrospection: Online Inspection and Attribution

Retrospection turns the deployed model’s own production conversations
into failure evidence that is reliable enough to learn from (requirement
R1), and decides whose failure each one is before any of them can
influence training (R2). It runs continuously, around the clock, on the
traffic served by the in-house model. Its screening, analysis, review,
and attribution steps are run by an external frontier model rather than
by the in-house model
(Section [3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 What the loop depends on ‣ 3 Problem Formulation ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")),
so the deployed model never judges its own conversations. It is
deliberately separate from the evaluation system of
Section [7](#S7 "7 Evaluation System and Promotion ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents"):
online inspection discovers failures to learn from, whereas the
evaluation system measures candidate versions on fixed test sets. The
two use the same inspection procedure but never share cases or
denominators.

### 5.1 Continuous online inspection

Online inspection examines the production conversations handled by the
in-house model as they mature, 24 hours a day. Because no verifier
exists, inspection is organized as a sequence of separable decisions
rather than a single judge score
(Figure [3](#S5.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 5.1 Continuous online inspection ‣ 5 Retrospection: Online Inspection and Attribution ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")).
Three separations run through the design: discovering a suspicious
conversation is separate from confirming a Bad Case, a model’s judgment
is separate from the act of publishing it, and local evidence is
separate from production writes.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 3: Online inspection and attribution. Production conversations of
the in-house model are frozen into a case set $`\mathcal{Q}_{t}`$ and
pass an evidence-blinded inspection
(Eq. [18](#S5.E18 "In Freezing and evidence blinding. ‣ 5.1 Continuous online inspection ‣ 5 Retrospection: Online Inspection and Attribution ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents"))
that separates ranking, capacity-aware admission from three strata
(Eq. [20](#S5.E20 "In Capacity-aware admission. ‣ 5.1 Continuous online inspection ‣ 5 Retrospection: Online Inspection and Attribution ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")),
analysis, and independent review with reconciliation, and ends in one of
four terminal states
(Eq. [21](#S5.E21 "In Review, reconciliation, and gate. ‣ 5.1 Continuous online inspection ‣ 5 Retrospection: Online Inspection and Attribution ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")).
Terminal states feed back to the screener
(Eq. [23](#S5.E23 "In Feedback to the screener. ‣ 5.1 Continuous online inspection ‣ 5 Retrospection: Online Inspection and Attribution ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")).
Only confirmed failures reach attribution, which routes
model-attributable cases, together with their diagnosis $`d`$, to
incremental task construction, routes component failures to repair, and
holds cases whose cause cannot be isolated.

#### Freezing and evidence blinding.

Each inspection run first freezes its input: the source window or
report, the case identities, and the evidence view. We write
$`\mathcal{Q}_{t}`$ for the frozen case set of window $`t`$; online it
holds the mature conversations served by $`\pi_{\theta_{k}}`$ in that
window, and offline it is a fixed test set. Every case
$`x\in\mathcal{Q}_{t}`$ carries an evidence view $`\xi(x)`$ (dialogue,
tool calls and results, order state, trajectory, and the applicable
policy knowledge) and metadata $`\mu(x)`$ (source quality labels and
scores, report and model identities, experiment labels, and release-side
fields). The metadata are kept for auditing but never enter a judgment
prompt, so every judgment stage $`h`$ (screening, analysis, review) is
counterfactually invariant to them:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
h\bigl(\xi(x),\mu\bigr)=h\bigl(\xi(x),\mu^{\prime}\bigr)\qquad\text{for all metadata }\mu,\mu^{\prime}.
``` |  | (18) |

Scenario identity is taken from stable fields (test contract, region,
business group, scenario definition) rather than from the model’s reply.
Without
Eq. ([18](#S5.E18 "In Freezing and evidence blinding. ‣ 5.1 Continuous online inspection ‣ 5 Retrospection: Online Inspection and Attribution ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")),
a judge that knew the source system had failed a trace, or which version
produced it, could learn a label shortcut instead of judging the
behavior.

#### Screening as evidence grading.

A screening model compresses $`\mathcal{Q}_{t}`$ into a ranked candidate
pool. It is an evidence grader and ranker, not the final judge. For each
case it returns a suspicion score $`s(x)\in[0,1]`$ together with an
evidence profile: whether the defect is visible, the number of locatable
evidence anchors $`a(x)`$, the likelihood $`u(x)`$ that the case
survives to publication, and the degree $`\rho(x)`$ to which the verdict
depends on runtime evidence missing from the log. Only cases with strong
evidence are eligible for high-confidence admission,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{Q}^{\mathrm{el}}_{t}=\bigl\{x\in\mathcal{Q}_{t}:\;\text{defect visible},\;a(x)\geq a_{\min},\;u(x)\geq u_{\min},\;\rho(x)\leq\rho_{\max}\bigr\}.
``` |  | (19) |

Weak signals such as low satisfaction, long dialogue, or repeated
requests for a human may raise $`s(x)`$ but cannot establish eligibility
on their own. A case on which screening fails is not routed onward by
any fallback, so an infrastructure fault is never converted into an
apparent business risk.

#### Capacity-aware admission.

Deep analysis, review, and gating are expensive, and the choice of which
cases receive them shapes what the system can conclude. Admission
therefore fills a rolling capacity $`B_{t}`$ from three strata,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{Q}^{\mathrm{adm}}_{t}=\mathcal{Q}^{\mathrm{hi}}_{t}\cup\mathcal{Q}^{\mathrm{bd}}_{t}\cup\mathcal{Q}^{\mathrm{ex}}_{t},\qquad\bigl|\mathcal{Q}^{\mathrm{adm}}_{t}\bigr|\leq B_{t},
``` |  | (20) |

where $`\mathcal{Q}^{\mathrm{hi}}_{t}`$ takes the highest-scoring cases
of $`\mathcal{Q}^{\mathrm{el}}_{t}`$ to maximize immediate discovery,
$`\mathcal{Q}^{\mathrm{bd}}_{t}`$ samples the boundary band
$`\{x:|s(x)-\eta|\leq\beta\}`$ around the screening threshold $`\eta`$
to measure where the screener is uncertain, and
$`\mathcal{Q}^{\mathrm{ex}}_{t}`$ samples low-score or rare strata to
keep new failure families discoverable. Pure top-$`K`$ admission would
entrench the screener’s historical bias, and pure random admission would
spend expensive capacity on uninformative cases. Every admitted case is
committed to reach a terminal state; a suspicious case outside
$`\mathcal{Q}^{\mathrm{adm}}_{t}`$ carries no such commitment.

#### Deep analysis.

Each admitted case receives a structured case record that answers six
questions: what the user actually requested; which intent, FAQ, Skill,
or SOP path the system selected; which actions or promises the agent
made at the key turns; whether those violated regional, business-line,
compensation, risk-control, or language rules; whether the runtime
evidence suffices to support that judgment; and, if a defect exists, its
type, likely cause, and a suggested fix. A claim ledger links every
conclusion of the record to anchors in $`\xi(x)`$, and mechanical
contract checks verify the record’s structure. These auxiliary checks
improve consistency but never short-circuit the semantic review and
gate.

#### Review, reconciliation, and gate.

An independent reviewer, distinct from the analyst, challenges the
record against the policy knowledge base and returns a verdict
$`\omega(x)\in\{\textsc{bad},\textsc{expected},\textsc{inconclusive}\}`$.
Evidence gaps, malformed records, or conflicting conclusions send the
record back for reconciliation before the verdict is final. A
publication gate $`G(x)\in\{0,1\}`$ then requires a unique anomalous
turn, a complete evidence package, a valid problem classification, and
an explicit verdict. The terminal state $`\psi(x)`$ of an admitted case
is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\psi(x)=\begin{cases}\textsc{bad}&\text{if }\omega(x)=\textsc{bad}\text{ and }G(x)=1,\\
\textsc{expected}&\text{if }\omega(x)=\textsc{expected},\\
\textsc{fail}&\text{if review or infrastructure fails},\\
\textsc{inconclusive}&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}
``` |  | (21) |

The rule is fail-closed: a case that cannot be confirmed is recorded as
inconclusive or sent for manual review, and a review or gate pass is
never assumed. Only $`\psi(x)=\textsc{bad}`$ can reach learning.

#### Audit and the confirmed-bad rate.

An audit checks that every admitted case reached a terminal state, that
every confirmed case holds both a review and a gate pass, that expected
and inconclusive verdicts are backed by an independent review, that no
source label leaked into a prompt, and that denominators are consistent.
With
$`\mathcal{B}_{t}=\{x\in\mathcal{Q}^{\mathrm{adm}}_{t}:\psi(x)=\textsc{bad}\}`$,
the headline metric is the confirmed-bad rate over the complete frozen
set,

|     |                                                              |     |      |
|-----|--------------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       \widehat{R}_{t}=\frac{|\mathcal{B}_{t}|}{|\mathcal{Q}_{t}|}.
       ```                                                           |     | (22) |

Cases that were never admitted, and inconclusive cases, count neither as
failures nor as passes. If confirmation is precise, that is,
$`\mathcal{B}_{t}\subseteq\mathcal{B}^{\star}_{t}`$ for the set
$`\mathcal{B}^{\star}_{t}`$ of truly defective cases, then
$`\widehat{R}_{t}\leq|\mathcal{B}^{\star}_{t}|/|\mathcal{Q}_{t}|`$:
$`\widehat{R}_{t}`$ is a conservative lower bound on the defect rate
rather than a calibrated estimate of it. Online, it is a monitoring
signal over shifting traffic; versions are compared instead with the
offline inspection test of
Section [7.2](#S7.SS2 "7.2 Offline inspection test ‣ 7 Evaluation System and Promotion ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents"),
which applies the same procedure to a fixed case set.

#### Feedback to the screener.

Terminal states also recalibrate the inspection system itself. Writing
$`\mathcal{F}^{+}_{t}`$ and $`\mathcal{F}^{-}_{t}`$ for the screener’s
positive and negative examples,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{F}^{+}_{t+1}=\mathcal{F}^{+}_{t}\cup\mathcal{B}_{t},\qquad\mathcal{F}^{-}_{t+1}=\mathcal{F}^{-}_{t}\cup\{x\in\mathcal{Q}^{\mathrm{adm}}_{t}:\psi(x)=\textsc{expected}\}.
``` |  | (23) |

Inconclusive and failed cases enter neither set: a review failure is
semantically undecided, and an infrastructure failure says nothing about
model quality, so a broken evaluator is never learned as evidence of
safe behavior. The boundary and exploration strata of
Eq. ([20](#S5.E20 "In Capacity-aware admission. ‣ 5.1 Continuous online inspection ‣ 5 Retrospection: Online Inspection and Attribution ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents"))
supply the cases from which new failure families enter
$`\mathcal{F}^{+}`$. Inspection modes and the stage contract are
summarized in
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Inspection Details ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents"),
and
Appendix [C.1](#A3.SS1 "C.1 Two inspected production cases ‣ Appendix C Inspection Details ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")
follows two production conversations through the procedure, one judged
expected behavior and one confirmed as a Bad Case.

### 5.2 Failure attribution

A confirmed failure says that something went wrong, not that the model
should change. Attribution assigns responsibility before learning. It
assembles an evidence package for each confirmed case: the complete
trajectory, the executed tool results, the Skill/SOP, prompt, and tool
definitions the model was given and their recent changes, the training
coverage of similar situations, and the version of the judge involved.
Candidate causes and their repair routes are listed in
Table [2](#S5.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 5.2 Failure attribution ‣ 5 Retrospection: Online Inspection and Attribution ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents").

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
| Cause |  Evidence sought |  Route |
| Model behavior |  Same context and valid tools; the decision error is reproducible, including in situations that training covered poorly |  Incremental task and attribution-guided OPSD |
| Skill/SOP or prompt |  The policy or prompt itself is wrong, ambiguous, or inconsistent |  Revise the Skill/SOP or prompt |
| Tool, harness, or router |  Schema, dispatch, projection, or route mismatch |  Runtime repair |
| Judge or inspection |  Unsupported verdict or review disagreement |  Recalibrate the evaluator; discard the label |
| Infrastructure |  Timeout, missing artifact, failed write |  Operational recovery; no quality label |

Table 2: Attribution categories and repair routes. Only the
model-behavior category produces training data for Phase II; every other
category is repaired outside the model.

Co-occurrence is not causation: a concurrent Skill change does not by
itself make a failure the Skill’s fault, and the absence of similar
examples from training does not by itself explain a model error. Where
feasible, attribution performs controlled replay that varies the model,
the Skill/SOP and prompt, and the tool or harness contract
independently, and it retains a multi-cause or unknown label when the
cause cannot be isolated. This conservatism prevents the loop from
teaching the model to work around a broken tool or a miscalibrated
judge, which would be a self-confirming failure of exactly the kind RSI
must avoid.

For a model-attributable case, attribution emits a diagnosis $`d`$
alongside the route. The diagnosis records the supported cause,
including whether similar situations were scarce in training, the policy
and context under which the correct behavior is defined, the evidence
anchors, the decision point at which the model went wrong, and
corrective guidance. Recording the decision point matters for learning:
the guidance must be actionable with the information available at that
point, so that the model is not taught to assert outcomes it could not
have known. Because the correct action depends on the SOP in force, the
diagnosis is defined relative to the Skill/SOP the model was given when
the failure occurred.

## 6 Phase II: Evolve by Attribution-Guided On-Policy Self-Distillation

The evolve stage converts model-attributable failures into a weight
update (requirement R3). It has three parts. *Retrospective repair
construction* turns each failure into a verified repair at the first
decision where the model went wrong. *On-policy self-distillation*
trains the model on its own outputs at that decision against a teacher
that is the model itself, given the hindsight as privileged information.
*Data selection* balances the training signal and deliberately mixes
policy versions (R4). The resulting candidate is then evaluated and
promoted as described in
Section [7](#S7 "7 Evaluation System and Promotion ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents");
Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ 6.3 Data selection and mixing across policy versions ‣ 6 Phase II: Evolve by Attribution-Guided On-Policy Self-Distillation ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")
summarizes one full iteration.

### 6.1 From failures to verified repair tuples

A confirmed failure arrives as a long multi-turn trajectory, logged
across several streams (the requests sent to the model, the agent’s
outputs and tool calls, state persistence, and what the user saw),
together with a retrospective diagnosis. It cannot be used for training
as it stands, because it records the whole conversation, whereas the
model made each decision from only what preceded it. Everything from the
first error onward is therefore hindsight: the later turns are
conditioned on a state that a corrected policy would never reach, so
their correction is ill-defined, and the outcome and inspection that
exposed the failure were not available when the model erred.
Construction accordingly works at the single decision where the model
first went wrong, and separates the input the model had there from what
was learned afterwards
(Figure [4](#S6.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 6.1 From failures to verified repair tuples ‣ 6 Phase II: Evolve by Attribution-Guided On-Policy Self-Distillation ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")).

Let $`h_{t}`$ denote the exact input of the model at step $`t`$: the
message history, the tool schemas, the Skill content, and the generation
settings of that request. It is the agent’s information set at the
moment of decision. Everything that retrospection adds beyond $`h_{t}`$
is *hindsight*.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 4: Retrospective repair construction. (a) A confirmed failure is
cut at the first decision the model got wrong. Everything the model
could see at that moment becomes the student input; the erroneous
output, the rest of the conversation, the outcome, and the diagnosis
become hindsight. (b) The proposer uses hindsight to write a minimal
repair that remains justified by the decision-time input alone, an
independent verifier accepts or rejects it, and each accepted tuple can
be projected into SFT, DPO, or OPSD data. Every case ends in exactly one
terminal state.

#### Step 1: localize the first model error.

Let $`\mathcal{A}^{\star}(h_{t},c)`$ be the set of acceptable actions at
step $`t`$ under context $`c`$. Construction anchors the earliest
defective decision,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
t^{\star}=\min\bigl\{t:\;a_{t}\notin\mathcal{A}^{\star}(h_{t},c)\bigr\},
``` |  | (24) |

and proceeds only if attribution assigns this defect to the model. If
the earliest defect belongs to a tool, a state resolver, or an upstream
component, the case is routed to component repair even when later model
errors exist, since those later decisions were made on a corrupted
state. The anchor is identified by the request identity and the exact
logged output rather than by ordinal position, and a case without a
unique anchor is held as pending.

#### Step 2: causal truncation.

The training input is the exact request at the anchored decision,
$`x=h_{t^{\star}}`$: the message history up to but excluding
$`a_{t^{\star}}`$, with every other request field kept verbatim. The
erroneous output $`a^{-}=a_{t^{\star}}`$, everything after it, the
outcome $`z`$, and the diagnosis $`d`$ form the hindsight
$`\mathcal{H}=(a^{-},h_{>t^{\star}},z,d)`$, which may enter training
only on the teacher side.

#### Step 3: minimal counterfactual repair.

A proposer model receives $`x`$, $`a^{-}`$, the incident-time policy,
and the diagnosis $`d`$ (marked as invisible to the student), and
proposes a replacement $`a^{+}`$ for the single erroneous decision.
Writing $`\mathcal{M}(x)`$ for the actions whose asserted facts are
supported by $`x`$ alone, the proposer approximates the smallest
admissible edit,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
a^{+}\in\arg\min_{a\,\in\,\mathcal{A}^{\star}(x,c)\,\cap\,\mathcal{M}(x)}\;\delta\bigl(a,a^{-}\bigr),
``` |  | (25) |

where $`\delta`$ measures the extent of the change. Four constraints
make this precise. *Locality*: only the erroneous decision changes; the
prefix is identical, and nothing after the decision (tool results, user
replies, follow-up messages) is generated. *Feasibility*: $`a^{+}`$ uses
only the tools, arguments, and response fields available in $`x`$ under
context $`c`$. *Non-anticipation*: hindsight may tell the proposer
*that* $`a^{-}`$ was wrong, but it may not make $`a^{+}`$ more specific
than $`x`$ allows. For example, if a status tool returned only “not
picked up” and the original reply asserted that the food was still being
prepared, the repair may remove the unsupported claim but may not
substitute an order status observed later. *Compliance*: $`a^{+}`$
follows the policy in force at the time of the incident, not the current
one. When $`x`$ contains images, the proposer must consume the images
themselves.

#### Step 4: independent verification.

Deterministic checks first confirm prefix identity, a single in-place
difference, and schema validity of tool calls and response fields. An
independent verifier then judges $`(x,a^{-},a^{+},d)`$ along separate
axes: whether the target is a genuine model fault, whether the inspected
symptom is corrected, whether the repair stays at the decision boundary,
whether it complies with the incident-time policy, and whether it
respects the tool and format contract. A repair is accepted only if
every axis passes,
$`\mathrm{accept}=\bigwedge_{j}V_{j}(x,a^{-},a^{+},d)`$. Acceptance
certifies that $`a^{+}`$ is an acceptable decision at $`x`$; it does not
certify that a tool call would succeed or that the conversation would
end well.

#### Repair tuples and their training views.

Accepted cases form the incremental set

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\Delta_{k}=\bigl\{(x_{i},\,c_{i},\,a^{-}_{i},\,a^{+}_{i},\,d_{i},\,\ell_{i})\bigr\},
``` |  | (26) |

where $`\ell_{i}`$ links each tuple to its source case. One tuple
supports three training views
(Table [3](#S6.T3 "Table 3 ‣ Repair tuples and their training views. ‣ 6.1 From failures to verified repair tuples ‣ 6 Phase II: Evolve by Attribution-Guided On-Policy Self-Distillation ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")),
which we compare in
Section [8.6](#S8.SS6 "8.6 Ablation: how to learn from verified repairs ‣ 8 Experiments ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents").
Supervised fine-tuning imitates $`a^{+}`$, and direct preference
optimization \[[27](#bib.bib30)\] contrasts $`a^{+}`$ with $`a^{-}`$;
both treat a text written by the proposer as the target. OPSD instead
keeps the student on its own outputs and lets the reference reach it
only through the teacher. The construction resembles hindsight
relabeling \[[28](#bib.bib29)\] in that it reuses information that
becomes available only after the episode, but the hindsight is used to
correct the decision under the original goal, and it never reaches the
student.

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
| View | Student input |  Learning signal |
| SFT | $`x`$ |  imitate the reference repair $`a^{+}`$ |
| DPO | $`x`$ |  prefer $`a^{+}`$ over $`a^{-}`$ |
| OPSD | $`x`$ |  match a self-teacher that sees $`(x,I)`$, on the student’s own sampled output |

Table 3: Training views of a repair tuple $`(x,c,a^{-},a^{+},d)`$.
$`I=\mathrm{enc}(d,a^{-},a^{+})`$ is the privileged information.

#### Accounting.

Every case ends in exactly one terminal state: *admitted*, *routed* (the
first defect is not the model’s), *rejected* by the verifier, or
*pending* (no unique anchor, a failed construction, or unverified visual
evidence). Pending cases are never relabeled as rejected or routed, and
cases that are not admitted are not counted as failures the model cannot
learn. Before a tuple is used for training, four further checks apply:
the incident model is replayed at $`x`$ to test whether $`a^{-}`$
reproduces; the tuple is rendered with the target tokenizer, chat
template, tool schemas, and loss mask; the collator is verified to keep
$`I`$ out of the student input; and a minimal training run is executed.
Implementation details are given in
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Repair Construction Details ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents").

### 6.2 Hindsight as privileged information

For a tuple $`(x,c,a^{-},a^{+},d)\in\Delta_{k}`$, the student samples
its own decision at the anchored point,
$`\hat{y}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)`$: a single assistant turn, which
may contain a tool call; $`x`$ already encodes the context $`c`$. A
*self-teacher*, a frozen copy $`\bar{\theta}_{k}`$ of the model at the
start of the iteration, reads the same input with the privileged
information $`I=\mathrm{enc}(d,a^{-},a^{+})`$ added to its system
message, which states what went wrong, the SOP in force at the incident,
and the verified repair. The teacher then follows the student’s rollout
token by token
(Figure [5](#S6.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ A family of truncated KL losses. ‣ 6.2 Hindsight as privileged information ‣ 6 Phase II: Evolve by Attribution-Guided On-Policy Self-Distillation ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")),
so that at each position both models give a distribution over the whole
vocabulary from the same prefix,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
p_{\theta,t}=\pi_{\theta}\bigl(\cdot\mid x,\hat{y}_{<t}\bigr),\qquad q_{t}=\operatorname{sg}\!\left[\pi_{\bar{\theta}_{k}}\bigl(\cdot\mid x,I,\hat{y}_{<t}\bigr)\right],
``` |  | (27) |

where $`\operatorname{sg}`$ denotes stop-gradient. The objective
accumulates a divergence $`\ell_{t}`$ between the two over the student’s
own samples,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{OPSD}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{(x,I)\sim\Delta_{k}}\;\mathbb{E}_{\hat{y}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)}\Bigl[\sum_{t}m_{t}\,\ell_{t}(\theta)\Bigr],
``` |  | (28) |

where $`m_{t}`$ selects the generated tokens of the student’s turn and
excludes the prompt and padding. The rollout fixes the prefixes at which
the two models are compared and is then treated as data: the loss is
backpropagated directly through $`p_{\theta,t}`$, without a
policy-gradient estimator over the sampling step.

#### A family of truncated KL losses.

We define $`\ell_{t}`$ as a Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence restricted
to the tokens that matter to the teacher. Let $`\mathcal{S}^{K}_{t}`$ be
the $`K`$ tokens to which $`q_{t}`$ assigns the highest probability. The
family leaves three choices open: the direction of the divergence, the
size $`K`$, and a floor on negative token losses.
Section [8.7](#S8.SS7 "8.7 Ablation: OPSD loss ‣ 8 Experiments ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")
ablates all three. The configuration that we deploy uses the forward
direction with $`K=32`$ and the floor,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
u^{K}_{t}(\theta)=\sum_{v\in\mathcal{S}^{K}_{t}}q_{t}(v)\,\bigl[\log q_{t}(v)-\log p_{\theta,t}(v)\bigr],\qquad\ell_{t}(\theta)=\max\bigl(u^{K}_{t}(\theta),\,0\bigr).
``` |  | (29) |

Both distributions keep their full-vocabulary normalization: the $`K`$
terms are not renormalized, and no smoothing or lower bound is added to
the probabilities.

*Direction.* The forward direction weights each token by the teacher’s
probability. For $`u^{K}_{t}>0`$ its gradient is
$`-\sum_{v\in\mathcal{S}^{K}_{t}}q_{t}(v)\,\nabla_{\theta}\log p_{\theta,t}(v)`$,
a soft cross-entropy: the student is pulled toward every token that the
informed teacher finds plausible, in proportion to the teacher’s
confidence, instead of toward one fixed token. The alternative is the
reverse direction over $`\mathcal{S}^{K}_{t}`$ and one cell that merges
all remaining tokens,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\ell^{\mathrm{rev}}_{t}(\theta)=\sum_{c\,\in\,\mathcal{S}^{K}_{t}\cup\{\mathrm{tail}\}}p_{\theta,t}(c)\,\bigl[\log p_{\theta,t}(c)-\log q_{t}(c)\bigr],\qquad r(\mathrm{tail})=\sum_{v\notin\mathcal{S}^{K}_{t}}r(v)\;\text{ for }r\in\{p_{\theta,t},q_{t}\},
``` |  | (30) |

which is a proper KL divergence between the two distributions coarsened
to $`K+1`$ cells, and hence nonnegative. It is mode-seeking: it
penalizes the student for placing mass where the teacher does not,
rather than for missing mass where the teacher places it.

*Floor.* Without a tail cell, $`u^{K}_{t}`$ is only a partial sum of the
forward KL, and it can be negative although the full divergence cannot.
By the log-sum inequality, $`u^{K}_{t}\geq Q_{t}\log(Q_{t}/P_{t})`$,
where $`Q_{t}`$ and $`P_{t}`$ are the total probabilities that the
teacher and the student place on $`\mathcal{S}^{K}_{t}`$, so it is
negative only when the student already places more mass on the set than
the teacher does. Driving it lower would only concentrate the student
further: the minimizer of $`u^{K}_{t}`$ is $`q_{t}/Q_{t}`$ on the set,
with zero probability on every other token. The floor stops the update
of such a token at zero. It acts on the sum at each token, before
masking and averaging, not on individual terms or on the batch mean, and
it bounds a loss, not a probability.

*Batch loss.* Over a batch, the loss is the mean over all generated
tokens,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\hat{\mathcal{L}}(\theta)=\frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{tok}}}\sum_{i,t}m_{i,t}\,\ell_{i,t}(\theta),\qquad N_{\mathrm{tok}}=\sum_{i,t}m_{i,t},
``` |  | (31) |

so every generated token of the batch, tool-call syntax included, has
equal weight. No task reward, policy-gradient term, or auxiliary SFT or
DPO loss enters the update, and the forward objective needs from the
teacher only its $`K`$ most likely tokens and their probabilities at
each position. The configuration is listed in
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E OPSD Training Configuration ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents").

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 5: Attribution-guided on-policy self-distillation at the failing
decision. The student samples a fresh decision $`\hat{y}`$ from the
decision-time input $`x`$. A frozen copy of the same model, additionally
given the privileged information $`I`$ (diagnosis, incident-time SOP,
and verified repair), reads the same prefixes, so at every token
position both models give a distribution over the vocabulary. The loss
compares the two on the teacher’s top-$`K`$ tokens, in the forward
direction with a floor at zero in the deployed configuration, and is
backpropagated directly. Gradients flow only into the student, and $`I`$
stays on the teacher side of the privileged boundary. The direction of
the KL divergence, $`K`$, and the floor are ablated in
Section [8.7](#S8.SS7 "8.7 Ablation: OPSD loss ‣ 8 Experiments ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents").

Three properties make this objective a mechanism for grounded
self-improvement rather than for compression.

#### On-policy at the failing decision.

The model is corrected on what it would do now at the decision where it
failed, not on a text written by someone else. A fresh sample is drawn
for every update, so the same tuple yields different student turns in
different epochs, and the data never contain a fixed target sequence.
Supervised fine-tuning on $`a^{+}`$ is off-policy: it imitates the
surface form of the proposer’s output, which may be unlikely under the
model’s own distribution. Preference optimization contrasts two fixed
outputs, neither of which need be what the current model produces. OPSD
defines its targets on the student’s own sample, so the signal stays
relevant as the model changes, in line with on-policy distillation more
broadly \[[16](#bib.bib28), [17](#bib.bib22)\].

#### A teacher that is the model itself.

The teacher starts from the same weights as the student, so its targets
lie close to the student’s distribution and the update concentrates on
the decisions that the privileged information changes. Keeping it fixed
during the iteration, rather than tracking the student as a moving
average, anchors the signal: the student cannot move its own target.
This anchoring is what makes a small increment usable. The target at
every token is the model’s own distribution, so tokens that the
privileged information does not affect carry little loss, whereas a
fixed target text has to be fitted everywhere; on increments of this
size SFT and DPO collapse
(Section [8.6](#S8.SS6 "8.6 Ablation: how to learn from verified repairs ‣ 8 Experiments ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")).
The teacher’s only advantage over the student is $`I`$, in line with the
intuition that a capable model can rationalize verified privileged
information and teach its weaker, uninformed self \[[21](#bib.bib19),
[20](#bib.bib7)\]. In our implementation the repair proposer is a
frontier model (GPT-5.6-Sol). Its output reaches training only as a
verified reference inside $`I`$: the student never sees it and is never
trained to copy its wording. The proposer is a replaceable component,
and letting the in-house model propose its own repairs is a natural step
toward a more closed loop
(Section [9](#S9 "9 Discussion ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")).

#### Grounded privileged information.

The privileged information is neither an unverified solution nor the
model’s own critique. The failure is established by retrospection, its
cause by attribution, its location by first-error localization, and the
reference repair by an independent verifier; only the articulation of
the corrected behavior in the student’s own distribution is left to the
model. A self-critique loop would let the model’s biases define both the
problem and its correction.

The privileged information never crosses the privileged boundary. It is
not appended to student inputs, production requests, or held-out
evaluation, and the training data loader is checked to keep it out of
the student context, so measured improvement reflects what the model has
internalized. Because construction enforces non-anticipation, the
teacher’s targets remain actionable from $`x`$ alone, and because the
teacher scores the student’s own tokens, a different but acceptable
decision is not forced into the wording of $`a^{+}`$. The student’s
sample is a single turn: a tool call it produces is scored but not
executed. Letting the student continue the conversation in the simulator
after the repaired decision is a natural generalization that we leave to
future work.

#### Why not reinforcement learning from outcome rewards.

A natural alternative is to optimize the agent against an outcome
reward, for example with group-relative policy optimization
(GRPO) \[[29](#bib.bib31)\]. We deliberately do not, because no
available reward is faithful to the production objective. CARE is
ultimately judged by user satisfaction, and satisfaction is a poor
training reward: most conversations are never rated, ratings arrive only
at the end of a conversation, and they are confounded by factors outside
the agent’s decisions, such as courier delays, refund policy, and the
food itself. They also cannot be computed for a replayed or simulated
decision. Rewards that can be computed are either unrelated to
satisfaction, such as format or tool-validity checks, or produced by LLM
judges, which an optimizer can exploit \[[7](#bib.bib16)\]; rubric
rewards \[[30](#bib.bib5)\] make the criteria explicit but would still
have to be calibrated against satisfaction. OPSD avoids defining a
scalar reward altogether. Its token-level signal is the divergence from
a teacher that sees a verified repair, so learning is grounded in
reviewed evidence about specific decisions rather than in a proxy for
satisfaction.

### 6.3 Data selection and mixing across policy versions

Production failures are unevenly distributed: a few micro-scenarios,
such as repeated handoff requests or formulaic comfort replies, recur
many times with nearly identical repairs. Training on all of them would
spend most of the update on a handful of patterns. Before training,
repair tuples are therefore deduplicated per micro-scenario under a cap:
for the deployed model, repeated handoff micro-scenarios typically keep
at most two tuples and homogeneous comfort patterns at most five,
distinct compound errors are kept in full, and no further reweighting or
oversampling is applied.

The failures behind a set of repair tuples occur at different times, and
Skills and SOPs are revised in between, so a training set mixes several
policy versions. We keep this mixture by design. A tuple is a good
example not because its SOP is the newest, but because its repair
follows the SOP that its own input carries: the compliance constraint of
Section [6.1](#S6.SS1 "6.1 From failures to verified repair tuples ‣ 6 Phase II: Evolve by Attribution-Guided On-Policy Self-Distillation ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")
judges every repair against the policy in force when the failure
occurred, and that policy is part of $`x`$. Training on such a mixture
teaches the model to follow the SOP it is given and to generalize across
revisions, instead of memorizing one version that will soon be replaced.
The cold-start corpus follows the same principle
(Section [4.4](#S4.SS4 "4.4 Cold-start objective ‣ 4 Phase I: Cold Start from Production Traces ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")).
Tuples from superseded policies are therefore neither discarded nor
rewritten to the latest policy.

1: base parameters $`\theta_{\mathrm{base}}`$; production traces $`D`$

2:
$`\theta_{0}\leftarrow\textsc{ColdStart}\bigl(\theta_{\mathrm{base}},\textsc{DataEngine}(D)\bigr)`$
