````math
## 7 Evaluation System and Promotion

Before a candidate replaces the deployed version, it is evaluated by an
evaluation system with two chained offline stages, and then compared
with the incumbent online
(Section [7.3](#S7.SS3 "7.3 Online comparison ‣ 7 Evaluation System and Promotion ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")).
The candidate first runs an executable simulation test
(Section [7.1](#S7.SS1 "7.1 Executable simulation test ‣ 7 Evaluation System and Promotion ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")),
which yields its simulation accuracy; the conversation traces it
produces there are then inspected offline
(Section [7.2](#S7.SS2 "7.2 Offline inspection test ‣ 7 Evaluation System and Promotion ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")),
which yields its inspection Bad Case rate. The simulation test is
compiled automatically from the latest Skill/SOP and then frozen, so
every candidate evaluated against it sees exactly the same cases, and
both scores are computed on the same runs. This separates evaluation
from the continuous online inspection of
Section [5.1](#S5.SS1 "5.1 Continuous online inspection ‣ 5 Retrospection: Online Inspection and Attribution ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents"),
whose cases change with the traffic and feed learning rather than
measurement.

### 7.1 Executable simulation test

A question-answering test treats the user’s message as a fixed input and
a single reply as the output, so it cannot separate saying the right
thing from getting the matter resolved. In customer service, information
is revealed over several turns, queries and business actions change the
state of orders and after-sales requests, and the user acts on what the
agent has done. A run must therefore answer three questions: what the
agent knew, that is, whether it obtained the facts it needed and which
remained uncertain; what it did, that is, the timing and order of its
queries, explanations, confirmations, and business actions; and what
resulted, that is, how the user’s situation and the business state
actually changed. The object under test is consequently a trajectory
produced under fixed conditions rather than a reply, and different
wording is acceptable whenever the process and the outcome satisfy the
rules. The simulation test realizes this as a closed loop: the
conditions of a case are fixed before the run, the simulated user, the
agent, and a simulated business world interact during it, and the
verdict is decided afterwards from what actually happened
(Figure [6](#S7.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 7.1 Executable simulation test ‣ 7 Evaluation System and Promotion ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")).
A keyword-matching mock cannot represent state that changes with actions
and time, and executing against production systems would introduce
sensitive data and uncontrolled side effects.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 6: The executable simulation environment. Before the run, the
frozen case is split into one view per module
(Eq. [38](#S7.E38 "In How a case reaches the modules. ‣ 7.1 Executable simulation test ‣ 7 Evaluation System and Promotion ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")):
the user simulator receives the user’s goal, initial knowledge, and
signal-gated reactions; the system simulator the initial state and event
schedule; the agent only its operating context; and the assessment the
branch and the oracle, which no participant sees
(Eq. [37](#S7.E37 "In Information boundary. ‣ 7.1 Executable simulation test ‣ 7 Evaluation System and Promotion ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")).
During the run, the orchestrator mediates every exchange, only the
system simulator changes business state, and each participant receives
its own projection of that state. After the run, the trace and the state
log are judged against the oracle, and each case ends in pass or fail
(Eq. [41](#S7.E41 "In Judgment. ‣ 7.1 Executable simulation test ‣ 7 Evaluation System and Promotion ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")).
The traces are also inspected offline
(Section [7.2](#S7.SS2 "7.2 Offline inspection test ‣ 7 Evaluation System and Promotion ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")).

#### Test cases and frozen conditions.

The $`j`$-th test case is the tuple

|     |                                                                |     |      |
|-----|----------------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       e_{j}=\bigl(\phi_{j},\;x_{j,0},\;c,\;b_{j},\;\Omega_{j}\bigr),
       ```                                                             |     | (32) |

where $`\phi_{j}`$ is the user’s situation (why the user makes contact,
what the user knows at the start, and what the user wants resolved),
$`x_{j,0}`$ is the initial business state of
Eq. ([2](#S3.E2 "In 3.1 Agents, policies in context, and the incumbent ‣ 3 Problem Formulation ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")),
including events that are scheduled but have not yet occurred, $`c`$ is
the operating context of
Eq. ([1](#S3.E1 "In 3.1 Agents, policies in context, and the incumbent ‣ 3 Problem Formulation ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents"))
under which the case is compiled, $`b_{j}`$ is the decision branch that
the case targets, and $`\Omega_{j}`$ is its acceptance oracle. All
components must refer to the same Skill/SOP version, and a case with a
missing component is not compiled rather than being completed from
defaults. Freezing a case fixes its starting point and its acceptance
criteria, not the dialogue: everything after the first turn is
determined by the actions actually taken. A frozen test
$`\mathcal{Z}=\{e_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N}`$ is run with the same user simulator,
transition rules, tool set, run budget, and judging procedure for every
candidate, so that a difference between two candidates’ results can be
attributed to the agents rather than to the conditions.

#### Branch-driven scenarios.

The unit of coverage is a decision branch, a point at which a fact or an
action changes what the correct decision is, rather than a paraphrase of
the user’s request. A user who reports that an order has not arrived
does not by that statement determine the correct reply: the order query
may return that the order is still being delivered, or that it was
delivered although the user denies receiving it, and the Skill/SOP may
require different handling in the two cases. A pair of cases that differ
only in this result tests whether the agent decides from the queried
fact rather than giving one answer to every report of a missing order.
Each branch closes a five-link chain,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\text{reachable state}\;\to\;\text{observable signal}\;\to\;\text{user reaction}\;\to\;\text{agent decision}\;\to\;\text{post-run evidence},
``` |  | (33) |

and a missing link produces false coverage: a branch can be listed in
the plan while its signal never appears in a run, or the agent can make
the decision while no evidence shows on what basis and with what effect.

#### Closed-loop dynamics.

Each case is executed in a partially observable environment with two
participants,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{E}=\bigl(\mathcal{X},\,A_{\mathrm{u}},\,A_{\mathrm{c}},\,T,\,O_{\mathrm{u}},\,O_{\mathrm{c}},\,\Omega\bigr),
``` |  | (34) |

where $`\mathcal{X}`$ is the space of business states,
$`A_{\mathrm{u}}`$ the user’s utterances and operations,
$`A_{\mathrm{c}}`$ the agent’s replies, queries, and business actions,
$`T`$ the transition function, $`O_{\mathrm{u}}`$ and $`O_{\mathrm{c}}`$
the user- and agent-visible projections of the state, and $`\Omega`$ the
acceptance oracle. At turn $`t`$ the user and the agent act on their own
histories, and the business world advances on the actions that actually
occurred and on the elapsed virtual time $`\Delta_{t}`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
a^{\mathrm{u}}_{t}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{u}}\bigl(\cdot\mid h^{\mathrm{u}}_{t},\phi_{j}\bigr),\qquad a_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}\bigl(\cdot\mid h_{t},c\bigr),\qquad x_{t+1}=T\bigl(x_{t},\,a^{\mathrm{u}}_{t},\,a_{t},\,\Delta_{t}\bigr).
``` |  | (35) |

A user action states a request, supplies information, or operates a card
that has been shown; an agent action is a reply, a query, or a business
action, as in
Eq. ([2](#S3.E2 "In 3.1 Agents, policies in context, and the incumbent ‣ 3 Problem Formulation ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")).
The transition function is the only way the state changes. A query
returns information and leaves $`x_{t}`$ unchanged; a refund or
cancellation exists only if a registered and validated action was
executed by the system simulator; and an agent’s statement that
something has been done is not a transition. Each request returns an
explicit *executed*, *business-rejected*, or *protocol-failed* outcome,
which is the result $`y_{t}`$ of
Eq. ([2](#S3.E2 "In 3.1 Agents, policies in context, and the incumbent ‣ 3 Problem Formulation ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")),
and a repeated request does not apply the same change twice. Scheduled
events, such as the completion of a refund review, take effect only when
the virtual clock passes them. Because $`T`$ and the event schedule are
deterministic, variation across repeated runs of a case comes from the
two language models and not from the environment. In
Figure [6](#S7.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 7.1 Executable simulation test ‣ 7 Evaluation System and Promotion ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents"),
the scenario compiler produces $`e_{j}`$, the user simulator implements
$`\pi_{\mathrm{u}}`$, the system simulator holds $`x_{t}`$ and
implements $`T`$, and the orchestrator is the only component that
sequences turns, advances the virtual clock, and ends the run.
Table [4](#S7.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Closed-loop dynamics. ‣ 7.1 Executable simulation test ‣ 7 Evaluation System and Promotion ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")
lists what each role may and may not do.

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
| Role |  May |  May not |
| Scenario compiler |  Fix the user situation, initial state, Skill/SOP version, branch, and oracle |  Choose an action for the agent during the run |
| User simulator |  Speak, confirm, or operate on what has been shown |  Read $`x_{t}`$ or $`\Omega_{j}`$ |
| System simulator |  Hold $`x_{t}`$, execute actions, advance virtual time |  Infer a state change from the agent’s wording |
| Agent under test |  Query, decide, reply, and act |  Observe $`x_{t}`$ other than through query results, or see $`\Omega_{j}`$ |
| Post-run assessment |  Judge from $`\Omega_{j}`$ and the recorded evidence |  Steer any participant during the run |

Table 4: Roles in a simulation run. Each role has a fixed boundary.

#### Information boundary.

The business state is never shown to either participant. The user and
the agent each receive their own projection of it,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
o^{\mathrm{u}}_{t}=O_{\mathrm{u}}\bigl(x_{t};\,\text{content displayed to the user}\bigr),\qquad o_{t}=O_{\mathrm{c}}\bigl(x_{t};\,\text{results returned to the agent}\bigr),
``` |  | (36) |

and the histories $`h^{\mathrm{u}}_{t}`$ and $`h_{t}`$ accumulate only
their owner’s observations and actions. The two windows differ: that the
system holds an order status does not mean that the user has seen it,
and an agent that has not yet queried cannot answer from the hidden
state. The acceptance oracle is read only after the run, so a run
depends on its case only through the starting conditions,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\tau_{j}\sim P\bigl(\cdot\mid\phi_{j},\,x_{j,0},\,c;\;\pi_{\mathrm{u}},\,\pi_{\theta},\,T\bigr),
``` |  | (37) |

in which $`\Omega_{j}`$ does not appear, and the branch $`b_{j}`$ enters
only through the state and user situation that realize it.
Eq. ([37](#S7.E37 "In Information boundary. ‣ 7.1 Executable simulation test ‣ 7 Evaluation System and Promotion ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents"))
is the simulation counterpart of the evidence blinding of
Eq. ([18](#S5.E18 "In Freezing and evidence blinding. ‣ 5.1 Continuous online inspection ‣ 5 Retrospection: Online Inspection and Attribution ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")).
It excludes two self-confirming loops: a simulated user that reveals a
result the agent has not yet produced, so that the agent reaches the
expected answer by being told it, and an environment that advances the
state along the expected path, so that an agent passes without acting.

#### How a case reaches the modules.

The compiled case is never handed to any module as a whole. Before the
run, the orchestrator splits $`e_{j}`$ into one view per module,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\underbrace{\phi_{j}}_{\text{user simulator}},\qquad\underbrace{x_{j,0}}_{\text{system simulator}},\qquad\underbrace{c}_{\text{agent}},\qquad\underbrace{(b_{j},\,\Omega_{j})}_{\text{assessment}},
``` |  | (38) |

and keeps the case identity, the run budget $`L`$, and the termination
rules for itself. The system simulator thus knows the truth but not what
is expected of the agent; the user simulator knows the user’s goal and
what the user would say in response to particular signals, but neither
the business state nor the branch under test; the agent is configured
with its operating context only and learns about the case solely through
the user’s messages and its own query results; and the branch and the
oracle reside with the assessment, which reads them after the run. No
module that acts during the run therefore holds $`\Omega_{j}`$, which is
what makes
Eq. ([37](#S7.E37 "In Information boundary. ‣ 7.1 Executable simulation test ‣ 7 Evaluation System and Promotion ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents"))
hold by construction. A branch is accordingly not transmitted as one
object but realized jointly: each link of the chain in
Eq. ([33](#S7.E33 "In Branch-driven scenarios. ‣ 7.1 Executable simulation test ‣ 7 Evaluation System and Promotion ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents"))
is placed in the module that owns it, and the branch is reached only if
the interaction connects them.
Table [5](#S7.T5 "Table 5 ‣ How a case reaches the modules. ‣ 7.1 Executable simulation test ‣ 7 Evaluation System and Promotion ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")
traces this distribution for one branch.

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
| Link |  Placed in |  Example |
| Reachable state |  System simulator, in $`x_{j,0}`$ |  The order is recorded as delivered |
| Observable signal |  Projections $`O_{\mathrm{c}}`$ and $`O_{\mathrm{u}}`$ |  The order query returns *delivered* to the agent; the user learns it only when the agent says so or a card shows it |
| User reaction |  User simulator, as a gated pair $`(\sigma_{\ell},r_{\ell})`$ in $`\phi_{j}`$ |  Once told that the order was delivered, the user states that nothing was received |
| Agent decision |  Not given to the agent; checked by $`\Omega^{\mathrm{req}}_{j}`$ and $`\Omega^{\mathrm{pro}}_{j}`$ |  Whether the agent queries before answering, and how it then handles a disputed delivery |
| Post-run evidence |  Assessment, from the trace and the state log |  The query and its result, the agent’s statements, and any executed action with its state change |

Table 5: How the five links of a branch
(Eq. [33](#S7.E33 "In Branch-driven scenarios. ‣ 7.1 Executable simulation test ‣ 7 Evaluation System and Promotion ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents"))
are placed in the modules, for the branch in which an order is recorded
as delivered while the user reports that it has not arrived. The example
illustrates the distribution only; the correct handling is whatever the
Skill/SOP in force specifies.

#### Information-limited user simulation.

The user simulator is goal-directed but sees only what a real user would
see: messages, cards, and page results. Its view of the case is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\phi_{j}=\bigl(g_{j},\;k^{0}_{j},\;\{(\sigma_{\ell},r_{\ell})\}_{\ell}\bigr),
``` |  | (39) |

consisting of a goal $`g_{j}`$, the knowledge $`k^{0}_{j}`$ that the
user has at the start, and reactions $`r_{\ell}`$, each attached to a
signal $`\sigma_{\ell}`$ that a user could observe, such as being told
that the order was delivered or being shown a card. A reaction becomes
available only after its signal has appeared in the user’s history, so
the knowledge the simulator may use at turn $`t`$ is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
K_{t}=k^{0}_{j}\cup\bigl\{r_{\ell}:\;\sigma_{\ell}\text{ occurs in }h^{\mathrm{u}}_{t}\bigr\},\qquad\pi_{\mathrm{u}}\bigl(\cdot\mid h^{\mathrm{u}}_{t},\phi_{j}\bigr)=\pi_{\mathrm{u}}\bigl(\cdot\mid h^{\mathrm{u}}_{t},g_{j},K_{t}\bigr).
``` |  | (40) |

This is how a branch reaches the user: not as a script or a target, but
as a reaction that the agent’s behavior or a business event has to
unlock. If the signal never occurs, the reaction is never used and the
branch is not reached in that run. The simulator keeps a persistent
session, so the user can maintain a request across turns, remember what
the agent promised, and react to new information. Besides speaking, it
has two capabilities: reading $`K_{t}`$, and requesting an operation
that has been displayed, such as a click or a confirmation, whose effect
is decided by $`T`$. Its wording may vary from run to run, but its
knowledge may not exceed $`K_{t}`$ and $`h^{\mathrm{u}}_{t}`$: it may
not use $`r_{\ell}`$ before $`\sigma_{\ell}`$ has occurred, or operate
content that was never shown.

1: frozen case $`e_{j}`$; candidate $`\pi_{\theta}`$; run budget $`L`$

2: load $`x_{j,0}`$, $`\phi_{j}`$, and $`c`$ into their modules; hold
$`(b_{j},\Omega_{j})`$ $`\triangleright`$
Eq. ([38](#S7.E38 "In How a case reaches the modules. ‣ 7.1 Executable simulation test ‣ 7 Evaluation System and Promotion ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents"))

3: $`t\leftarrow 0`$;  $`a^{\mathrm{u}}_{0}\leftarrow`$ opening message
from $`g_{j}`$ and $`k^{0}_{j}`$

4: repeat

5:   deliver $`a^{\mathrm{u}}_{t}`$ to the agent

6:   repeat$`\triangleright`$ one agent turn

7:    $`a\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid h_{t},c)`$

8:    if $`a`$ is a query or a business action then

9:      system simulator executes $`a`$ under $`T`$; append $`y_{t}`$
and $`O_{\mathrm{c}}`$ to $`h_{t}`$    

10:   until $`a`$ is a reply to the user

11:   deliver the reply and any card through $`O_{\mathrm{u}}`$; update
$`K_{t+1}`$ $`\triangleright`$
Eq. ([40](#S7.E40 "In Information-limited user simulation. ‣ 7.1 Executable simulation test ‣ 7 Evaluation System and Promotion ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents"))

12:
  $`a^{\mathrm{u}}_{t+1}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{u}}(\cdot\mid h^{\mathrm{u}}_{t+1},g_{j},K_{t+1})`$;
an operation is executed under $`T`$

13:   if the conversation waits, advance the virtual clock and fire due
events

14:   $`t\leftarrow t+1`$

15: until the user closes the conversation, the agent transfers it, or
$`t=L`$

16: assemble the trace $`\tau_{j}`$ and the state log

17: judge $`Y_{j}`$ by
Eq. ([41](#S7.E41 "In Judgment. ‣ 7.1 Executable simulation test ‣ 7 Evaluation System and Promotion ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")):
pass if $`Y_{j}=1`$, else fail

Algorithm 2 Running one simulation case

#### Running one case.

Algorithm [2](#alg2 "Algorithm 2 ‣ Information-limited user simulation. ‣ 7.1 Executable simulation test ‣ 7 Evaluation System and Promotion ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")
lists the steps of one run. The orchestrator first loads each view of
Eq. ([38](#S7.E38 "In How a case reaches the modules. ‣ 7.1 Executable simulation test ‣ 7 Evaluation System and Promotion ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents"))
into its module. The user simulator opens with a message formed from
$`g_{j}`$ and $`k^{0}_{j}`$ alone, for example that the order has not
arrived. The agent then takes a turn that may contain several steps: the
orchestrator sends each query or business action to the system
simulator, which executes it under $`T`$ and returns the outcome
$`y_{t}`$ together with the agent’s projection, until the agent replies
to the user. The orchestrator delivers the reply and any card to the
user through $`O_{\mathrm{u}}`$; if this produces a signal
$`\sigma_{\ell}`$, the corresponding reaction $`r_{\ell}`$ enters
$`K_{t}`$. The user then answers, asks, or operates a displayed control,
and any operation is again executed by the system simulator. When the
conversation has to wait, for example for a review in progress, the
orchestrator advances the virtual clock and the system simulator fires
the events that fall due, whose user-visible effects reach the user
through $`O_{\mathrm{u}}`$. The loop ends when the user closes the
conversation, the agent transfers it to a human, or the budget $`L`$ is
exhausted, and the trace and the state log are then judged as described
next. In the example of
Table [5](#S7.T5 "Table 5 ‣ How a case reaches the modules. ‣ 7.1 Executable simulation test ‣ 7 Evaluation System and Promotion ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents"),
the five links are connected in order: the agent’s query exposes the
delivered state, its reply passes the signal to the user, the unlocked
reaction makes the user deny receipt, the agent’s subsequent handling is
the decision under test, and the trace and the state log hold the
evidence. An agent that answers without querying never exposes the
signal, so the branch is not reached, and the run is judged on what the
agent actually did, for instance asserting a delivery status it never
checked.

#### Judgment.

Every case ends in one of two outcomes, pass or fail, decided from the
recorded trace and the final business state. The oracle is decomposed as
$`\Omega_{j}=(\Omega^{\mathrm{req}}_{j},\Omega^{\mathrm{pro}}_{j},\Omega^{\mathrm{goal}}_{j})`$,
and

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
Y_{j}=\mathbf{1}\bigl\{\Omega^{\mathrm{req}}_{j}(\tau_{j})\;\wedge\;\neg\,\Omega^{\mathrm{pro}}_{j}(\tau_{j})\;\wedge\;\Omega^{\mathrm{goal}}_{j}(\bar{x}_{j})\bigr\},
``` |  | (41) |

with pass exactly when $`Y_{j}=1`$. A run that does not meet all three
conditions is a fail, including one that ends without the evidence to
show that they hold. The required-step condition
$`\Omega^{\mathrm{req}}_{j}`$ checks the classification of the request
and the timing and order of the necessary steps, such as querying before
asserting a fact or obtaining confirmation before a business action;
where a goal admits several legitimate paths it accepts any of them, so
it constrains paths rather than prescribing a script. The prohibition
condition $`\Omega^{\mathrm{pro}}_{j}`$ detects behavior that the
Skill/SOP forbids, such as promising a compensation the policy does not
allow or reporting an action that was never executed. The goal condition
$`\Omega^{\mathrm{goal}}_{j}`$ is evaluated on the final business state
$`\bar{x}_{j}`$, not on the agent’s account of it. Wording, politeness,
and language quality are not part of $`Y_{j}`$; they are judged by the
offline inspection of
Section [7.2](#S7.SS2 "7.2 Offline inspection test ‣ 7 Evaluation System and Promotion ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents"),
and a fluent reply cannot compensate for a wrong action or an unresolved
outcome.

#### Simulation accuracy.

The simulation accuracy is the share of the frozen test that passes,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{sim}}(\theta)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}Y_{j}(\theta),
``` |  | (42) |

and it is the term that enters the combined score of
Eq. ([45](#S7.E45 "In 7.4 Promotion ‣ 7 Evaluation System and Promotion ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")).
Branches are counted by whether they were reached rather than whether
they were planned: with $`\mathcal{J}`$ the branches that the test plans
to exercise, the branches covered by a candidate are

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{J}^{\mathrm{hit}}(\theta)=\bigl\{b\in\mathcal{J}:\;b\text{ is reached in }\tau_{j}\text{ for some }j\bigr\}.
``` |  | (43) |

#### Comparing candidates.

Two candidates $`\theta_{A}`$ and $`\theta_{B}`$ face the same frozen
test, Skill/SOP version, observation boundaries, and run budget. Because
the environment responds to the agent, the two may reach different
states and conversations from the same start; this divergence is the
behavior under test, and their dialogues are not forced into a common
script. They are compared case by case,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\Delta_{B-A}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\bigl(Y_{j}(\theta_{B})-Y_{j}(\theta_{A})\bigr).
``` |  | (44) |

Results obtained on tests compiled from different Skill/SOP versions, or
under a different definition of success, are not a controlled
comparison.

#### Test compilation and scope.

Whenever the Skill/SOP changes, the scenario compiler regenerates the
simulation test from the latest version automatically: it enumerates the
business branches that the new policy defines and compiles a test case
of the form of
Eq. ([32](#S7.E32 "In Test cases and frozen conditions. ‣ 7.1 Executable simulation test ‣ 7 Evaluation System and Promotion ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents"))
for each. The compiled set is then frozen, and all candidates evaluated
in that period run against the same static set. A result therefore
supports a bounded conclusion: on these cases, under this Skill/SOP
version, and with this evidence, the candidate passed a given share of
the cases. Its validity rests on four conditions: the cases cover the
branches that matter, and many cases do not by themselves imply good
branch coverage; the oracle agrees with the rules in force and never
guides the agent during the run; the simulated user acts only on what it
has seen while keeping a natural range of expression; and the business
state changes only through executed actions and time. The result does
not extrapolate to satisfaction on production traffic, which is why a
candidate is also compared online
(Section [7.3](#S7.SS3 "7.3 Online comparison ‣ 7 Evaluation System and Promotion ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents"));
the fidelity of the simulator is discussed in
Section [9](#S9 "9 Discussion ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents").
Execution tiers and experimental controls are detailed in
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Simulation Environment Details ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents").

### 7.2 Offline inspection test

The offline inspection test takes the traces that a candidate produced
in the simulation test and judges them with the inspection procedure of
Section [5.1](#S5.SS1 "5.1 Continuous online inspection ‣ 5 Retrospection: Online Inspection and Attribution ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents"),
in the offline mode that freezes the traces and the evidence view
(Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Inspection Details ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")).
The two stages are complementary. The simulation oracle checks business
outcomes
(Eq. ([41](#S7.E41 "In Judgment. ‣ 7.1 Executable simulation test ‣ 7 Evaluation System and Promotion ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents"))):
whether the required steps were taken, whether a prohibited action
occurred, and whether the required state change happened. The inspection
judges every decision along the way, including service quality,
language, and policy compliance in replies, so a trace that reaches the
right outcome can still contain a Bad Case. Because the traces come from
the frozen simulation test, the resulting confirmed-bad rate
$`\widehat{R}`$ of
Eq. ([22](#S5.E22 "In Audit and the confirmed-bad rate. ‣ 5.1 Continuous online inspection ‣ 5 Retrospection: Online Inspection and Attribution ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")),
the *inspection Bad Case rate*, has a fixed denominator and is
comparable across candidates, unlike the rate observed by online
inspection.

### 7.3 Online comparison

A candidate that passes offline evaluation serves part of the production
traffic while the incumbent serves the rest at the same time. The
primary online metric is user satisfaction, compared against the
incumbent in the same period; the escalation rate to human staff is
monitored as a secondary signal, since an appropriate handoff is a
correct outcome.

### 7.4 Promotion

The two offline scores are combined into a single evaluation score,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
S(\theta)=\tfrac{1}{2}\Bigl[\mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{sim}}(\theta)+\bigl(100-\widehat{R}(\theta)\bigr)\Bigr],
``` |  | (45) |

where $`\mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{sim}}`$ is the simulation accuracy of
Eq. ([42](#S7.E42 "In Simulation accuracy. ‣ 7.1 Executable simulation test ‣ 7 Evaluation System and Promotion ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents"))
and $`\widehat{R}`$ the inspection Bad Case rate, both percentages
measured on the current frozen simulation test, so that $`S`$ rewards a
high simulation accuracy and a low inspection Bad Case rate equally. A
candidate $`\theta^{\prime}`$ replaces the deployed version
$`\theta_{k}`$ only if it is at least at parity on the combined score,

|     |                                          |     |      |
|-----|------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       S(\theta^{\prime})\;\geq\;S(\theta_{k}),
       ```                                       |     | (46) |

and it is then confirmed online against the incumbent. Using one
combined score rather than two separate conditions accepts a candidate
whose small loss on one score is outweighed by a larger gain on the
other, while still requiring the evaluation as a whole not to regress.
Promotion to production requires human approval, which makes CARE a
human-on-the-loop system in the sense of
Section [2.1](#S2.SS1 "2.1 Recursive Self-Improvement ‣ 2 Background and Related Work ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents"),
and the previous version remains available as a fallback. Because the
test sets are compiled from the latest Skill/SOP, a candidate is
evaluated against the policy currently in force, not against earlier
policy versions;
Section [9](#S9 "9 Discussion ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")
discusses this limitation.

## 8 Experiments

We evaluate CARE over five recursive iterations in a production
deployment and ask five questions. Does the recursive phase keep
improving the in-house model, offline and online
(Section [8.2](#S8.SS2 "8.2 Recursive improvement over five iterations ‣ 8 Experiments ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents"))?
How does the final model compare with the incumbent and other frontier
models
(Section [8.3](#S8.SS3 "8.3 Comparison with other models ‣ 8 Experiments ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents"))?
How do the versions fare with real users
(Section [8.4](#S8.SS4 "8.4 Online deployment by scenario ‣ 8 Experiments ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents"))?
What does the final model take to serve
(Section [8.5](#S8.SS5 "8.5 Serving latency and cost ‣ 8 Experiments ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents"))?
And which design choices matter when learning from repairs
(Sections [8.6](#S8.SS6 "8.6 Ablation: how to learn from verified repairs ‣ 8 Experiments ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")–[8.7](#S8.SS7 "8.7 Ablation: OPSD loss ‣ 8 Experiments ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents"))?

### 8.1 Setup

#### Deployment.

The agent handles after-sales customer service for a food-delivery
platform in seven regions: Saudi Arabia (SA), Brazil (BR), Hong Kong
(HK), and the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Kuwait, and Qatar, which
form the GCC4 group. Typical scenarios include missing or wrong items,
cold food and poor taste, spillage and damage, non-receipt, delivery
delays, refunds, and cancellations. The agent uses Skills and tools for
order lookup, compensation, refunds, and handoff to human staff, and
serves several languages.

#### Models.

The incumbent is GPT-5.4, which served production before replacement.
Our in-house model, CARE-31B, is post-trained from the open-weight
Gemma-4-31B-IT: CARE-31B V0 is the cold-start model of
Section [4](#S4 "4 Phase I: Cold Start from Production Traces ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents"),
and V1–V5 are produced by five Phase II iterations, each with its own
round of incremental repair data. As references we evaluate GPT-6-Luna,
Gemini-3.5-Flash, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, Qwen3.8-27B, and the untuned
Gemma-4-31B-IT, all without task-specific training. The harness around
the model is maintained by engineering and differs between versions, for
instance when a harness defect is fixed, so the absolute results of a
version can reflect harness changes as well as the model. Each change
applies to CARE-31B and the incumbent at the same time, so the
difference between the two in the same period is not affected.

#### Offline evaluation.

Both offline metrics come from the evaluation system of
Section [7](#S7 "7 Evaluation System and Promotion ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents"),
not from the online inspection that supplies training failures.
*Simulation accuracy* is $`\mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{sim}}`$ of
Eq. ([42](#S7.E42 "In Simulation accuracy. ‣ 7.1 Executable simulation test ‣ 7 Evaluation System and Promotion ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")),
the share of the cases in the frozen simulation test of
Section [7.1](#S7.SS1 "7.1 Executable simulation test ‣ 7 Evaluation System and Promotion ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")
that pass. The *inspection Bad Case rate* is the confirmed-bad rate
$`\widehat{R}`$ of
Eq. ([22](#S5.E22 "In Audit and the confirmed-bad rate. ‣ 5.1 Continuous online inspection ‣ 5 Retrospection: Online Inspection and Attribution ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents"))
obtained by inspecting the same simulation traces offline
(Section [7.2](#S7.SS2 "7.2 Offline inspection test ‣ 7 Evaluation System and Promotion ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents"));
lower is better, and it is a conservative observed rate rather than a
calibrated population error rate. All versions and reference models are
evaluated on the same frozen test of 559 cases.

#### Online evaluation.

In all seven regions, production traffic is split between CARE-31B and
the incumbent, each serving part of the users at the same time, so the
incumbent in the same period serves as the concurrent control. Each
version served one period (P1–P6 in
Table [6](#S8.T6 "Table 6 ‣ 8.2 Recursive improvement over five iterations ‣ 8 Experiments ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")).
The primary online metric is *satisfaction*, the share of 4–5 star
ratings among valid 1–5 star ratings of agent-handled conversations.
Conversations are assigned to periods by their start time in local time.
Ratings are sparse, so we report 95% Wilson intervals and two-sided
two-proportion tests.

Table [6](#S8.T6 "Table 6 ‣ 8.2 Recursive improvement over five iterations ‣ 8 Experiments ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")
and
Figure [7](#S8.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ 8.2 Recursive improvement over five iterations ‣ 8 Experiments ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")
follow the six versions. Cold start makes the base model competent at
the task but not yet safe enough to replace the incumbent. V0 completes
93.0% of simulated cases, against 79.0% for the untuned Gemma-4-31B-IT,
yet its inspection Bad Case rate of 6.42% is higher than that of both
the untuned base (5.59%) and the incumbent (4.60%), and online it trails
the incumbent by 4.6 points of satisfaction ($`p=0.03`$). Imitating
historical traces teaches the model to act within the business process,
but not to avoid the errors that appear only once it acts on its own,
which is the gap the recursive phase is designed to close.

#### Offline.

The first iteration lowers the Bad Case rate from 6.42% to 4.35%, V4
reaches 4.11%, and V5 reaches 1.97%, 69% below V0 and less than half of
the incumbent’s 4.60%. Simulation accuracy rises from 93.0% to a peak of
95.30% at V3 and stands at 94.10% for V5, 2.7 points below the
incumbent. The two scores do not improve in lockstep: the Bad Case rate
rises from V1 to V2, simulation accuracy dips slightly from V3 to V4,
and V5 gives up 1.07 points of simulation accuracy against V4 for a drop
of 2.14 points in the Bad Case rate. Each iteration learns from the
failures of the version before it, so its effect concentrates on newly
observed failure families. The combined score of
Eq. ([45](#S7.E45 "In 7.4 Promotion ‣ 7 Evaluation System and Promotion ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")),
on which promotion is decided, never decreases: it rises from 93.29 for
V0 to 96.07 for V5, against 96.10 for the incumbent.

#### Online.

The satisfaction gap closes over the same iterations
(Figure [7](#S8.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ 8.2 Recursive improvement over five iterations ‣ 8 Experiments ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")a).
The early versions trail the incumbent by 3.1 to 8.0 points; V4 matches
it ($`+0.34`$ points), and V5’s point estimate exceeds it ($`+1.73`$
points). Neither of the last two differences is statistically
significant ($`p=0.85`$ and $`p=0.47`$), so the correct reading is that
the in-house model reaches parity with the incumbent in user
satisfaction after five iterations, with point estimates at or above it.

### 8.4 Online deployment by scenario

Both arms vary from period to period because traffic composition, the
harness, and operating context change over time; this is why each
version is compared only with the incumbent in the same period. In P6,
CARE-31B matches or exceeds the incumbent’s satisfaction in the largest
scenario, meal-handover issues ($`+0.97`$ points), as well as in late
delivery ($`+4.33`$) and food quality ($`+5.87`$), while it trails
slightly in refunds and compensation ($`-3.29`$) and order acceptance
($`-1.78`$). Per-scenario rating counts are small, so these differences
are indicative only.

machine cost. The saving does not require full replacement: half of the
traffic already lowers the cost by 35.8%.

### 8.6 Ablation: how to learn from verified repairs

A repair tuple can be turned into training signal in several ways
(Table [3](#S6.T3 "Table 3 ‣ Repair tuples and their training views. ‣ 6.1 From failures to verified repair tuples ‣ 6 Phase II: Evolve by Attribution-Guided On-Policy Self-Distillation ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")).
We compare OPSD in its deployed configuration with two objectives that
train on fixed texts: SFT, which imitates the reference repair
$`a^{+}`$, and DPO \[[27](#bib.bib30)\], which prefers $`a^{+}`$ over
the erroneous output $`a^{-}`$. All three start from V4 and use the same
repair tuples and training budget, so the comparison isolates where the
learning signal is defined: on fixed texts, or on the outputs the model
actually produces. We do not include reinforcement learning from outcome
rewards, such as GRPO \[[29](#bib.bib31)\], because no reward is
available that tracks the production objective of user satisfaction
(Section [6.2](#S6.SS2.SSS0.Px5 "Why not reinforcement learning from outcome rewards. ‣ 6.2 Hindsight as privileged information ‣ 6 Phase II: Evolve by Attribution-Guided On-Policy Self-Distillation ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")).

|  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| Objective | Learning signal | On-policy | Sim. acc. (%) $`\uparrow`$ | Bad Case (%) $`\downarrow`$ | $`S`$ $`\uparrow`$ |
| SFT | imitate $`a^{+}`$ | $`\times`$ | – | – | – |
| DPO | prefer $`a^{+}`$ over $`a^{-}`$ | $`\times`$ | 15.1 | 1.88 | 56.61 |
| OPSD (CARE) | match self-teacher given $`I`$ | ✓ | 94.1 | 1.97 | 96.07 |

Table 9: Ablation of the learning signal. All objectives start from V4
and use the same repair tuples and training budget. *On-policy*: the
loss is defined on the model’s own samples. $`S`$ is the combined score
of
Eq. ([45](#S7.E45 "In 7.4 Promotion ‣ 7 Evaluation System and Promotion ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")).
A dash means unavailable, not zero: SFT collapsed during training and
never entered the full test. The OPSD row is configuration 4 of
Table [10](#S8.T10 "Table 10 ‣ 8.7 Ablation: OPSD loss ‣ 8 Experiments ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents").

Table [9](#S8.T9 "Table 9 ‣ 8.6 Ablation: how to learn from verified repairs ‣ 8 Experiments ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")
shows that both fixed-text objectives collapse on an increment of this
size. SFT does not yield a usable model: incremental training
destabilizes it until it emits tool calls continuously, it is stopped by
a one-case smoke test, and it never enters the full test. DPO completes
training but collapses in behavior, handing the conversation to a human
in the first turn: its simulation accuracy is 15.1%, against 95.17% for
V4 before the update and 94.1% for OPSD. Its Bad Case rate of 1.88% is
low only because a conversation that is handed off at once leaves few
decisions to get wrong, which is why promotion weighs both scores: the
combined score of DPO is 56.61, against 96.07 for OPSD.

We read this as a consequence of training on fixed texts at this data
scale rather than of SFT as such. The same negative log-likelihood
trains V0 stably in cold start
(Section [4.4](#S4.SS4 "4.4 Cold-start objective ‣ 4 Phase I: Cold Start from Production Traces ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents"))
on a corpus about fifty times larger than the increment. A few hundred
repair tuples cannot constrain a full-parameter update toward fixed
texts: every token of those texts is fitted, and nothing holds the
model’s behavior in place elsewhere. In OPSD the target at every token
is the model’s own distribution, reshaped only where the privileged
information applies, so the same data corrects decisions without
destabilizing the model. Small increments are the normal operating
condition of the recursive phase, so this stability is a precondition
for the loop, not a secondary benefit.

The OPSD objective of
Section [6.2](#S6.SS2 "6.2 Hindsight as privileged information ‣ 6 Phase II: Evolve by Attribution-Guided On-Policy Self-Distillation ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")
leaves three choices open: the direction of the KL divergence, the
truncation size $`K`$, and the floor on negative token losses.

compares four configurations. Configuration 1 uses the reverse
divergence of
Eq. ([30](#S6.E30 "In A family of truncated KL losses. ‣ 6.2 Hindsight as privileged information ‣ 6 Phase II: Evolve by Attribution-Guided On-Policy Self-Distillation ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents"))
over the top 128 tokens and a tail cell. Configurations 2, 3, and 4 use
the forward partial sum of
Eq. ([29](#S6.E29 "In A family of truncated KL losses. ‣ 6.2 Hindsight as privileged information ‣ 6 Phase II: Evolve by Attribution-Guided On-Policy Self-Distillation ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")):
configuration 2 with $`K=128`$ and the floor, configuration 3 with
$`K=128`$ and no floor, and configuration 4 with $`K=32`$ and the floor.
All four start from V4 with V4 as the frozen teacher, train for three
epochs (210 steps) on the same 280 repair tuples, and are evaluated at
the third epoch. The remaining settings are shared
(Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E OPSD Training Configuration ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")):

| Config. | Direction | $`K`$ | Tail | Floor | Sim. acc. (%) $`\uparrow`$ | Bad Case (%) $`\downarrow`$ | $`S`$ $`\uparrow`$ |

| 2 | forward, Eq. ([29](#S6.E29 "In A family of truncated KL losses. ‣ 6.2 Hindsight as privileged information ‣ 6 Phase II: Evolve by Attribution-Guided On-Policy Self-Distillation ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")) | 128 | – | ✓ | 93.0 | 2.87 (16) | 95.07 |
| 3 | forward, Eq. ([29](#S6.E29 "In A family of truncated KL losses. ‣ 6.2 Hindsight as privileged information ‣ 6 Phase II: Evolve by Attribution-Guided On-Policy Self-Distillation ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")) | 128 | – | – | 94.1 | 2.50 (14) | 95.80 |
| 4 | forward, Eq. ([29](#S6.E29 "In A family of truncated KL losses. ‣ 6.2 Hindsight as privileged information ‣ 6 Phase II: Evolve by Attribution-Guided On-Policy Self-Distillation ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")) | 32 | – | ✓ | 94.1 | 1.97 (11) | 96.07 |

Table 10: Ablation of the OPSD loss. *Bad Case*: confirmed Bad Cases
over all cases of the report, with their number in parentheses. $`S`$ is
the combined score of
Eq. ([45](#S7.E45 "In 7.4 Promotion ‣ 7 Evaluation System and Promotion ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")).

Configuration 4 is the best overall and the one deployed as V5: it
matches the highest simulation accuracy (94.1%) and has the highest
combined score (96.07). Two comparisons change a single factor. From
configuration 2 to 4, $`K`$ falls from 128 to 32, which raises the
simulation accuracy by 1.1 points and the combined score by 1.00. From
configuration 2 to 3, the floor is removed at $`K=128`$, which raises
the simulation accuracy by 1.1 points and the combined score by 0.73. We
do not extrapolate from these two values of $`K`$ to a claim that
smaller is better. The other two comparisons change several factors at
once and therefore do not support a single-factor reading: configuration
1 to 4 (+1.51 in combined score) replaces the reverse top-128 loss with
its tail cell by the forward top-32 partial sum and adds the floor, and
configuration 3 to 4 (+0.27) changes both $`K`$ and the floor. The
effect of the KL direction alone is thus not isolated by this design.
Configuration 1 shows the trade-off that the combined score resolves: it
has the lowest Bad Case rate (1.79%), but also the lowest simulation
accuracy (90.9%), and with it the lowest combined score (94.56).

These differences rank the configurations but are not significance
claims. The Bad Case counts are the retained counts of separate review
batches: those of configurations 1 and 2 did not pass final batch
acceptance, those of configurations 3 and 4 were not re-reviewed under
later rulings, and configuration 4 has one further undetermined case
that is not counted. A gap of a few cases, such as 10 against 11 between
configurations 1 and 4 or 14 against 11 between configurations 3 and 4,
should therefore not be read as a difference between them.

## 9 Discussion

### 9.1 RSI as an industrial learning workflow

The contribution of CARE is to operationalize RSI within a production
customer-service domain, connecting production feedback, failure
attribution, verified repair, and model updates under domain-specific
business rules. Failures encountered by the deployed model become
learning tasks only after evidence review and attribution.
Model-attributable failures feed OPSD with the model itself as teacher,
conditioned on privileged failure information, while component defects
are routed to repair. This division of responsibility directs
improvement to the part of the service that should change. Evaluation
and promotion connect each update back to the operating requirements of
the deployed system.

The multilingual food-delivery deployment provides evidence for this
workflow in a live business setting. Across five iterations, the
in-house 31B model’s inspection Bad Case rate fell below the
incumbent’s, and online user satisfaction reached parity. The recurring
process turns production experience into persistent model updates,
extending improvement beyond the one-time transfer of incumbent traces
used for cold start. These results support RSI as an operational
approach to improving a deployed domain-specific agent.

### 9.2 Evolving with business policies

Customer-service policies change independently of the learner, so
continued improvement requires adaptation to the Skill/SOP currently
supplied to the agent. CARE separates changes to business instructions
from changes to model behavior: component owners revise Skills/SOPs,
while model-attributable failures feed the learning loop. Training mixes
failures from historical SOP versions, each judged against the policy in
force when it occurred, so that following the given policy is the
learning objective. For promotion, simulation tests are compiled from
the latest SOP and frozen; offline inspection evaluates the resulting
traces, and the combined-score gate precedes online comparison and human
approval. This coupling of policy-conditioned learning and SOP-derived
evaluation is designed to shorten the turnaround from a business change
to a validated model update.

### 9.3 Why grounding keeps the loop from collapsing

Recursive training on a model’s own outputs is known to erode the tails
of its distribution \[[6](#bib.bib24)\], and loops in which a model
judges itself tend to reinforce its own errors \[[5](#bib.bib20)\]. CARE
faces both risks because it trains on its own rollouts and uses itself
as the teacher. Four design choices counter these risks. First, failures
are established through executed state and reviewed evidence, never
through the model’s opinion of its own output. Second, learning uses the
model’s own distribution, reshaped only where a verified diagnosis
applies, as its target, rather than raw self-generated text. Third,
allocation in cold start and capped selection in Phase II deliberately
preserve low-frequency regions and scenarios. Finally, promotion depends
on fixed test sets that are separate from the traffic used for learning
and evaluated without the diagnosis. Together, these choices keep the
loop in the regime that recent analyses describe as productive: bounded
improvement against an external anchor.

The ablations show the same effect from the other side. On a small
increment, objectives that train on fixed texts lose the model’s
behavior altogether: SFT collapses during training, and DPO collapses
into handing conversations to a human in the first turn
(Section [8.6](#S8.SS6 "8.6 Ablation: how to learn from verified repairs ‣ 8 Experiments ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")).
OPSD trains on the same data and stays stable, which we attribute to its
target being the model’s own distribution.

These design choices also define the method’s limits. The self-teacher
remains limited by what it can articulate from the privileged
information. A verified reference repair narrows this gap, but an
external model writes that repair in our implementation, and external
models also drive inspection and attribution, so the loop is not
self-contained
(Section [3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 What the loop depends on ‣ 3 Problem Formulation ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")).
Grounding comes from the verifier, not the proposer. Repairs are also
local to a single decision. Failures that reflect missing knowledge
rather than an incorrect decision are better addressed through component
repair (for example, a Skill revision), new cold-start data, or
human-written targets.

### 9.4 Limitations

The simulator is a modeled world, not a digital twin. Its state model,
user behavior, and rules can be wrong, and we have not yet measured its
fidelity against production in terms of user behavior, conversation
length, tool paths, and failure families. Work on L2 dialogue simulation
compares generated and human dialogue distributions while accounting for
speakers’ language backgrounds \[[31](#bib.bib32)\]. Adapting such
comparisons to customer-service interaction patterns is a direction for
validating our simulator.

The confirmed-bad rate depends on screening recall and is therefore a
conservative observed rate, not a calibrated population estimate. Its
calibration against multilingual human annotation remains to be
reported. The online results have few satisfaction ratings in the early
periods, while the offline metrics are reported without confidence
intervals. The serving cost does not include the research, storage,
network traffic, or additional operations staff of the in-house model,
so it understates the full cost of ownership. Harness changes between
versions overlap with the model updates, so the trend across versions
cannot be assigned to the model alone, although the comparison with the
incumbent within a period is not affected. The Bad Case counts behind
the loss ablation come from separate review batches that were not
uniformly finalized, and the ablation changes several factors at once in
some comparisons, so it supports a choice of configuration rather than
the effect of each factor. Attribution is itself a model-assisted
judgment, so its errors propagate into training. Controlled replay and
an explicit unknown category mitigate this risk, but attribution
accuracy is not reported here.

Evaluation is also bound to a single policy version. The simulation test
is compiled from the latest Skill/SOP and then frozen; offline
inspection evaluates the resulting simulation traces. A candidate is
therefore measured against the policy currently in force, not against
earlier versions. Although training mixes failures from several SOP
versions, we do not yet test whether a candidate still follows an
earlier SOP correctly when given that SOP as input. The benefit of
mixing versions is therefore argued rather than measured. How well a
deployed version follows a revision made after its training, and how
long a revision takes to reach a validated update, have not yet been
quantified. Since the simulation test is already compiled automatically
from a given SOP, a natural next step is to compile tests for several
SOP versions and evaluate each candidate across them. We plan this
cross-version simulation test as future work.

### 9.5 Risks and safeguards

- •
  Evaluator gaming. Repeated optimization against the same judge or the
  same exposed cases can raise scores without improving service. Cases
  used to construct incremental tasks are excluded from evaluation,
  judgments are evidence-blinded, and boundary and exploration samples
  continue to identify new failure families.
- •
  Privileged leakage. If the diagnosis were available to the student or
  during evaluation, measured gains would overstate what the model
  learned. By construction, the diagnosis is confined to the teacher
  context.
- •
  Forgetting. Training on new failures can erase behavior that earlier
  versions handled well. Static test sets detect such regressions only
  for the current SOP, making cross-version evaluation a priority for
  future work.
- •
  Privacy and authority. Production traces contain personal and order
  information. Collection, linking of human conversations, and
  publication require explicit authorization, de-identification,
  least-privilege access, and audit logs; credentials and customer
  identifiers never enter prompts or reports. Promotion is a
  consequential action approved by an accountable owner.

### 9.6 Toward a more closed loop

CARE is deliberately human-on-the-loop and relies on an external
frontier model for retrospection and construction. Several extensions
would further close the improvement loop. Having the current model
propose its own repairs under the same verifier would remove the
external proposer from Phase II; inspection, attribution, and
verification would remain external, because the grounding depends on
their independence from the model being improved. Allowing the student
to continue the conversation in the simulator after the repaired
decision would extend on-policy learning from single decisions to
multi-step recovery. Compiling simulation tests for several Skill/SOP
versions would allow each candidate to be evaluated across policy
revisions rather than only against the latest one. Rubric-based
reinforcement learning \[[30](#bib.bib5)\] could complement
self-distillation for failures whose correction is easier to verify than
to articulate, provided that hard business constraints cannot be offset
by soft rubric scores. Finally, co-evolving the evaluator with the
agent \[[32](#bib.bib18)\], under the same grounding discipline, would
let the retrospection stage improve alongside the model it inspects.

## 10 Conclusion

We presented CARE, a production framework for recursive self-improvement
in customer service. It aims to replace a frontier incumbent with an
in-house mid-sized model that learns from its own experience. A one-time
cold start on governed production traces made a 31B open-weight model
competent but left it with more confirmed failures than the incumbent.
Five recursive iterations then reduced its inspection Bad Case rate
below the incumbent’s and brought online user satisfaction to parity
with the incumbent. On small increments of repairs, training on fixed
target texts collapsed, whereas self-distillation remained stable, which
makes it the learning signal that the recursive phase depends on.

In each iteration, the model serves production traffic and its own
failures provide the next learning signal. A 24/7 online inspection
process establishes failures from reviewed evidence, and attribution
separates model errors from surrounding-system defects.
Model-attributable failures yield verified repairs for on-policy
self-distillation: the same model serves as teacher, with attribution
and repair available as privileged information withheld from the
student.

To support changing business requirements, Skills/SOPs enter through the
model’s input. Training mixes failures from several SOP versions, each
judged against the policy in force when it occurred, to teach the model
to follow the policy it is given. Evaluation uses a simulation test
compiled from the latest SOP and then frozen, followed by offline
inspection of its traces. The combined score must match or exceed that
of the deployed version before an online comparison with the incumbent
and promotion under human approval.

CARE thus makes continuing model evolution a practical production
process, designed to keep pace with business changes and shorten the
path from a revised policy to a validated update.

## Appendix A Cold-Start Details

### A.1 Evolution of the data recipe

The data engine of
Section [4](#S4 "4 Phase I: Cold Start from Production Traces ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")
is the result of several revisions, listed in
Table [11](#A1.T11 "Table 11 ‣ A.1 Evolution of the data recipe ‣ Appendix A Cold-Start Details ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents").
Early recipes concatenated complete human conversations (D2) or inserted
human turns into agent trajectories (D3–D6). Insertion aimed to improve
tone but risked introducing steps that the agent never took and facts
that only a human operator could know, which motivated protecting
business actions during insertion (D4), the precursor of
Eq. ([14](#S4.E14 "In Constrained rewrite. ‣ 4.3 State-aligned expression refinement ‣ 4 Phase I: Cold Start from Production Traces ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")),
and, eventually, the current rule of rewriting only existing turns
without adding messages. Rebalancing (D5) anticipated the hierarchical
allocation of
Section [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Hierarchical, capacity-constrained allocation ‣ 4 Phase I: Cold Start from Production Traces ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents"),
and the language repair of D7 anticipated the language admission checks.
The current engine replaces insertion with state-aligned refinement and
moves all screening before allocation.

|              |                                                           |
|--------------|-----------------------------------------------------------|
| Revision     |  Transformation                                           |
| D1 Baseline  |  Production incumbent trajectories, no human data         |
| D2 Concat    |  Append complete human-support conversations              |
| D3 Style     |  Filter, rewrite, and insert human turns                  |
| D4 Protect   |  Preserve business actions and metadata during insertion  |
| D5 Rebalance |  Adjust the region and scenario distribution              |
| D6 EvalPatch |  Target inspected failures while preserving structure     |
| D7 LangFix   |  Repair assistant language only                           |

Table 11: Historical revisions of the cold-start data recipe.

### A.2 Semantic screening states

Table [12](#A1.T12 "Table 12 ‣ A.2 Semantic screening states ‣ Appendix A Cold-Start Details ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")
defines the three verdicts of the semantic screening step. Screening
must cover the full structurally qualified pool with one-to-one identity
matching; missing results, duplicate identities, and inconsistent
assignments are treated as failures rather than passes. Disabling
screening yields a structurally qualified pool, not a pool that has
passed semantic screening.

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
| Verdict |  Meaning |  Effect |
| no_problem |  No supported execution defect; the decision does not depend on missing runtime evidence |  Admitted to allocation |
| problem |  Visible evidence supports a specific execution defect |  Quarantined |
| inconclusive |  No defect found, but the decision depends on missing decisive runtime evidence |  Quarantined separately |

Table 12: Semantic screening verdicts and their downstream effect.

### A.3 Training configuration

Table [13](#A1.T13 "Table 13 ‣ A.3 Training configuration ‣ Appendix A Cold-Start Details ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")
lists the configuration used to train V0 on $`D_{0}`$ with the objective
of
Eq. ([17](#S4.E17 "In 4.4 Cold-start objective ‣ 4 Phase I: Cold Start from Production Traces ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")).
The maximum sequence length matches the admission check of
Section [4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Admission ‣ 4 Phase I: Cold Start from Production Traces ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents"):
conversations longer than 16,384 tokens are excluded from $`D_{0}`$
rather than truncated.

|  |  |
|----|----|
|  Item |  Setting |
|  Base model |  Gemma-4-31B-IT |
|  Objective |  masked negative log-likelihood on assistant tokens (Eq. [17](#S4.E17 "In 4.4 Cold-start objective ‣ 4 Phase I: Cold Start from Production Traces ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")) |
|  Maximum sequence length |  16,384 tokens |
|  Epochs and steps |  one epoch; 467 steps |
|  Batch size |  global batch 32; micro-batch 1 per GPU |
|  Learning rate |  peak $`1\times 10^{-5}`$; warmup over 5% of steps (23 steps), then cosine decay |
|  Precision |  BF16 |
|  Hardware |  32 NVIDIA A100 80GB GPUs |

Table 13: Cold-start SFT configuration.

## Appendix B Simulation Environment Details

#### Execution tiers.

Simulation results are produced in three tiers with increasing scope
(Table [14](#A2.T14 "Table 14 ‣ Execution tiers. ‣ Appendix B Simulation Environment Details ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")).
An isolated execution error may be retried without changing the
experiment identity, and retries preserve attempt identity so that
failed executions are not silently dropped; global provider, version, or
aggregation failures stop the run.

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
| Tier |  Purpose |  Supported conclusion |
| Fixture smoke |  Check assets, protocols, state transitions, and the offline loop with a substitute agent |  Internal consistency of the environment |
| Live smoke |  Exercise a small slice with the real model, routes, and tools |  Integration evidence for that slice |
| Live end-to-end |  Run the real chain on a frozen scenario set |  Acceptance within the selected scope |

Table 14: Simulation execution tiers.

#### Experimental controls.

Controlled comparisons freeze the scenario set, capability versions,
simulator capabilities, route identity, user model, agent lifecycle, and
judgment contract. Version bindings, a compiled test plan, and a run
lock retain these identities, and detected drift stops execution instead
of substituting a runnable alternative with different semantics.

#### Evidence and privacy.

An attempt is the basic unit that joins user generation, system actions,
and agent calls into one local trace. Persistent reports retain redacted
identities, statuses, and references; raw prompts, full requests and
business state, credentials, and sensitive customer identifiers are
excluded.

## Appendix C Inspection Details

#### Inspection modes.

The inspection system exposes several modes that share prompts and
evidence schemas but keep independent queues, denominators, and side
effects
(Table [15](#A3.T15 "Table 15 ‣ Inspection modes. ‣ Appendix C Inspection Details ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")).
This separation prevents a local sample from becoming a population
denominator and a diagnostic screen from being reported as a
confirmed-bad rate.

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
| Mode |  Input and purpose |  Boundary |
| Online continuous |  Mature production sessions, for ongoing discovery |  Persistent source, ranked pool, admitted queue |
| Custom online |  A selected experiment, market, window, or user segment |  Independent of the main online queue |
| Offline check |  A frozen report or export with a fixed test set |  Frozen cases and evidence view |
| Screening only |  Fast candidate diagnosis |  No deep analysis or publication |
| Technical check |  Tool-call, log, and infrastructure anomalies |  Technical signal only; no semantic verdict |

Table 15: Inspection modes.

#### Stage contract.

Each stage of
Figure [3](#S5.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 5.1 Continuous online inspection ‣ 5 Retrospection: Online Inspection and Attribution ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")
produces a required artifact and can stop a case; a later stage cannot
manufacture evidence that an earlier one lacked
(Table [16](#A3.T16 "Table 16 ‣ Stage contract. ‣ Appendix C Inspection Details ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")).
Publication to the shared quality dashboard is incremental by test-set
version, requires a passing audit and explicit confirmation, and is
complete only after the written record has been read back and matched
against the intended payload.

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
| Stage |  Required artifact |  Stop condition |
| Freeze |  Source, case identities, evidence view |  Identity or snapshot not fixed |
| Screen |  Candidate score, evidence anchors, risk tier |  Screening failure |
| Admit |  Ranked pool and admitted queue |  Capacity or strata unavailable |
| Deep analysis |  Structured case record with claim ledger |  Unsupported claims |
| Review |  Independent verdict and correction history |  Conflict, missing evidence, malformed output |
| Gate and audit |  Terminal verdict, counts, denominator |  Missing field, count mismatch, leakage |

Table 16: Inspection stage contract.

#### Evaluation dimensions.

Business correctness covers routing, tool and action validity, process
progression, consistency between replies and actions, coverage of
available solutions, and appropriate escalation. Service quality covers
language consistency, emotion recognition, specific empathy, ownership,
and the absence of blaming or defensive language. Hard business
violations are reported separately from soft quality, and no aggregate
allows pleasant language to compensate for an invalid business action.

### C.1 Two inspected production cases

We follow two production conversations through the procedure of
Section [5.1](#S5.SS1 "5.1 Continuous online inspection ‣ 5 Retrospection: Online Inspection and Attribution ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents"):
one that the inspection judged correct and one it confirmed as a Bad
Case. Both are refund inquiries from consumer traffic in Saudi Arabia on
1 August 2026 (UTC), served by the in-house model during period P1 (V0)
under the same refund-consult Skill, and both were inspected in the
custom online mode of
Table [15](#A3.T15 "Table 15 ‣ Inspection modes. ‣ Appendix C Inspection Details ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents").
Dialogue is translated from Arabic and condensed; merchants and orders
are replaced by placeholders, with *Merchant A* the merchant the
customer means and *Merchant B* the merchant on the order card the
system suggests.

Two rules of the Skill decide both cases. When no order has been
selected, the agent calls a context resolver; if it returns no order ID,
the only allowed reply is ORDER_CONFIRMATION, asking the customer to
pick the order. If the customer says the current order is not the one
they mean, the agent must ask for the new order and must not reuse the
previous order’s result.
Table [17](#A3.T17 "Table 17 ‣ C.1 Two inspected production cases ‣ Appendix C Inspection Details ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")
summarizes the two cases.

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |  Case 1: expected behavior |  Case 2: confirmed Bad Case |
| Customer issue |  Refund for an order cancelled because the courier was late |  Charged, but the order was never confirmed |
| Retained window |  9 entries over 45 s |  15 entries over 5.5 min |
| Tool calls |  6: Skill load, context resolver |  8: Skill load, context resolver, order detail |
| Review |  First review FAIL; reconciled; second review PASS as expected behavior, high confidence |  First review PASS as confirmed Bad Case, high confidence |
| Gate and outcome |  Upload not allowed; closed as no issue |  Notification gate PASS; uploaded as a Bad Case |
| Inspection time |  26 min |  18.5 min |

Table 17: The two inspected cases at a glance.

#### Case 1: a suspicious-looking conversation judged correct.

Table [18](#A3.T18 "Table 18 ‣ Case 1: a suspicious-looking conversation judged correct. ‣ C.1 Two inspected production cases ‣ Appendix C Inspection Details ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")
lists the dialogue. The customer is frustrated, the agent never states a
refund status, and the order card it shows belongs to a different
merchant, all of which a judge relying on weak signals could read as a
failure. The inspection did not. In every turn after the Skill was
loaded, the resolver returned an empty order ID, so ORDER_CONFIRMATION
was the only path the Skill allowed; the agent neither guessed the order
nor claimed a refund state. The card on G09 is the order picker’s
initial suggestion, awaiting the customer’s confirmation, and the review
found that showing such a suggestion does not by itself violate the
picker’s design; the retained window ends before the customer confirms
any order. The first review failed the analysis; after reconciliation,
the second review passed it as expected behavior with no missing
evidence. Under
Eq. ([23](#S5.E23 "In Feedback to the screener. ‣ 5.1 Continuous online inspection ‣ 5 Retrospection: Online Inspection and Attribution ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")),
an expected verdict of this kind becomes a negative example for the
screener.

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| \# | Speaker |  Message (translated, condensed) |  Action and tools |
| G01 | Agent |  Welcome. Is your issue “When will I get my money back?” |  Entry FAQ |
| G02–03 | User |  No.  /  The Merchant A order. |  |
| G04 | Agent |  Do you mean an order from Merchant A? Please tell me the issue, e.g. a missing item, a wrong order, cold food, or a late delivery. |  INTENT_GUIDE |
| G05–07 | User |  I cancelled it and the money has not been returned.  /  The driver was late.  /  It has been over an hour and the money has not been returned. |  |
| G08 | Agent |  Since the order was cancelled because the driver was late, please confirm the order in the list and I will check its refund status. |  Skill loaded; resolver returns no order ID; ORDER_CONFIRMATION |
| G09 | Card |  Suggested order: Merchant B, delivered, 50.40 SAR, awaiting confirmation. |  |

Table 18: Case 1 dialogue (expected behavior). Replies the model
generated for G02, G05, and G06 were not delivered to the customer and
are omitted.

#### Case 2: a stale order kept after an explicit correction.

Table [19](#A3.T19 "Table 19 ‣ Case 2: a stale order kept after an explicit correction. ‣ C.1 Two inspected production cases ‣ Appendix C Inspection Details ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")
lists the dialogue. The customer names Merchant A in B05, yet in B06 the
agent looks up and reports on the Merchant B order, a delivered order
from three days earlier with no refund record. After the explicit
correction in B07, the reply B08 acknowledges in text that the customer
means a different order, but the confirmation card B09 still carries the
stale Merchant B order. The customer confirms that card (B10–B12), and
the conversation ends in a transfer to a human agent (B13–B15) without
the intended order ever having been checked. The review confirmed a
wrong-entity defect, the stale order and card after the correction, with
high confidence and no missing evidence; the gate passed and the case
was uploaded. The first erroneous turn is B06. The resolver also
returned the stale order ID in B06, B08, and B13, so the card shown in
B09 reflects runtime state as well as the model’s choice. Separating the
two is the task of attribution
(Section [5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2 Failure attribution ‣ 5 Retrospection: Online Inspection and Attribution ‣ CARE: Grounded Recursive Self-Improvementfor Production Customer-Service Agents")),
which decides whether such a case becomes training data.

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| \# | Speaker |  Message (translated, condensed) |  Action and tools |
| B01 | Agent |  Welcome. Is your issue “Why did the payment fail?” |  Entry FAQ |
| B02 | User |  I placed an order; the money was taken, but the order was not confirmed. |  |
| B03 | Agent |  Please select the order you are asking about, and I will check its payment or refund status. |  Skill loaded; resolver returns no order ID; ORDER_CONFIRMATION |
| B04 | Card |  Suggested order: Merchant B, delivered, 34.68 SAR, awaiting confirmation. |  |
| B05 | User |  I ordered from Merchant A and you took the money. Why was the order not confirmed? |  |
| B06 $`\times`$ | Agent |  I checked the Merchant B order: it was completed and delivered, and has no refund request. If this is not the right order, please give the order number. |  Resolver returns the Merchant B order; order detail: completed on 29 July, no after-sale record; GUIDE |
| B07 | User |  My order is not Merchant B; my new order is desserts from Merchant A. |  |
| B08 | Agent |  The order shown to me is from Merchant B, but you mean the new dessert order from Merchant A. Please select or confirm it. |  Resolver returns the Merchant B order again; ORDER_CONFIRMATION |

| B10–12 | User |  Clicks confirm on the card; “Yes.”; the system records the Merchant B order as confirmed. |  |
| B13 | Agent |  Sorry for the confusion. Since you confirmed this completed order, please contact a specialist, who can check the new Merchant A order directly. |  Resolver and order detail on the Merchant B order again; TRANSFER_TO_HUMAN |
| B14–15 | Agent, User |  Contact-a-specialist entry; the customer transfers to a human agent. |  |
````
